->(A mathematician of great fame during the reigns<-

## SOME SPIRITS:
->AIMING (HAD IT SUCCEEDED)<-
->To a general transformation of most STATES and<-
->KINGDOMS in the world.<-

->and PRINCES (some of whom were present at some of these<-

<header>Preface</header>

# PREFACE

What is presented here to you (Christian Reader) being a *True and Faithful Account, etc.* (as the title states, and as will be further clarified by this Preface), might be considered and called a "Work of Darkness" <note>The author acknowledges that communicating with spirits was often viewed as demonic or "dark" magic.</note> because of how it was conducted in some respects, as well as its very nature. Yet, it is nothing other than what was offered <note>original: "tendered"</note> with great care and caution to men of the highest dignity in Europe—kings and princes—and was listened to by all of them (except for those in England) for a while with great respect. 

It was gladly embraced and entertained by some for a long time; when the reputation of these events reached Rome, it caused the Pope to take action <note>original: "bestir himself"</note>, as he did not know what the outcome of it might be, or how much it might affect him. 

And indeed, it filled all people—both the learned and the unlearned in most places—with great wonder and astonishment. All of these things will be shown and proven <note>original: "made good"</note> (to the full extent of what I have said) within the contents of this book, supported by unquestionable records and evidence. And therefore I

<summary>Meric Casaubon introduces John Dee's records as a significant historical account that, despite its supernatural nature, was taken seriously by European monarchs and even drew the concerned attention of the Pope.</summary>
<keywords>Meric Casaubon, John Dee, Preface, Work of Darkness, European royalty, Papal reaction, credibility of spirits</keywords>

--- Page 3 ---
<meta>This page continues the author's justification for publishing the following work, emphasizing its utility in correcting religious delusions.</meta>

I have no doubt that enough men will be found in the world whose curiosity will lead them to read what I believe is unparalleled in its kind by any book that has been published in any age. I say this even if they read it for no other purpose than to satisfy their curiosity. But whatever other men, according to their various inclinations, may intend for themselves in reading it, I may and must here profess in the first place—in truth and sincerity—that the goal I propose for myself (so far as I have contributed to the publishing of this work) is not to satisfy curiosity, but to do good and promote religion. 

When we were first acquainted with the book and were offered the chance to read it, we had lately been occupied with a subject of much similarity: namely, the matter of mistaken inspiration and possession caused by ignorance of natural causes. <note>The author likely refers to his previous work on "Enthusiasm," which argued that many "divine" revelations were actually the result of physical or mental illness.</note> As our aim in publishing that previous labor was to do good, we have had good reason since to believe that we did not altogether miss what we aimed at, and so we could not help but gladly accept this book. 

As we gladly accepted it, we read it to the end with equal eagerness and speed. When we had finished, it was truly our opinion that publishing it would be very timely and useful. It is useful against atheists at all times, but especially in these times, when the spirit of error and illusion prevails so much. This is seen not only in professed Anabaptists <note>term: Anabaptists; here used as a derogatory label for radical religious groups perceived as socially and politically dangerous.</note> of the worst kind—whom former ages have known and abhorred—but also in many others. Though these others openly (and heartily, I hope, for most of them) disclaim and detest the fruits and effects that such causes have produced in others, they nevertheless ground themselves upon the same principles of supposed inspiration and imaginary revelations. On that account, they deem themselves, if not the only Christians, then much better Christians than others. 

I was much confirmed in this judgment when I was told (as indeed I was, at the start, by those who knew very well) that the most reverend, pious, and learned Archbishop of Armagh <note>James Ussher (1581–1656), a highly respected scholar and prelate.</note>, lately deceased, had declared the same opinion upon reading the said book before his death and wished it to be printed. 

However, because it is very possible that every reader will not at first be able to make good use of this sad story through rational inferences and observations, my chief aim in this preface is to help such readers. Furthermore, it is no less probable that this licentious age will produce many who, like the Sadducees of old (that is, Jewish Epicureans <note>note: original: "Jewish Epicures"; referring to those who deny the immortality of the soul and divine providence.</note>), believe in no spirit, angel, or resurrection. Therefore, being prepossessed with prejudice when they hear of...

<summary>The author argues that publishing this account of "revelations" is a religious duty intended to combat atheism and the dangerous delusions of radical sects who mistake natural phenomena for divine inspiration. He notes that the late Archbishop of Armagh also supported the book's publication.</summary>

--- Page 4 ---
<meta>This page continues the author's introductory argument regarding the existence of spirits and supernatural phenomena, addressing skeptics who dismiss such accounts as mere superstition or folly.</meta>

So many spirits as are mentioned here, and so many strange apparitions of various kinds, will not only cause some to reject these ideas, but will make them ready to laugh at anyone else who gives any credit to such things. I will not attempt to convert those who are committed to such an opinion because of a wicked life—that is, through unjust practices, luxurious and lewd behavior, or open profaneness disguised as "wit" and "gallantry" <note>original: "Wit and Galantry"; here meaning a fashionable, worldly, and often irreligious lifestyle</note>. I believe it is entirely just for God to leave such people to the error and blindness of their own judgments; therefore, without a miracle, there is little hope for them. 

However, I hope that those who are rational men, sober in their lives and conduct—such as I have known myself; men of excellent abilities in other matters, who are both willing to hear and able to consider—may receive some satisfaction from what I shall propose for their honest consideration. Were we to argue this case using the Bible, the matter would soon be settled. There is no other controversial point among men that I know of that could receive a more ample, full, clear, and speedy determination than this business of spirits, witches, and apparitions, if the Word of God were allowed to be the judge. 

But I will assume that I am dealing with those who, though they do not altogether deny the Word of God, will not easily admit anything they think is contrary to reason, or at least anything that cannot be supported by reason. I shall therefore refrain from all scriptural proofs and testimonies in this specific argument. I ask the Christian reader (who might otherwise rightly take offense at this omission) to take notice of the reason why I refrain. 

But though I will not use the Bible for proof, I hope I may be allowed to use some scriptural words by way of application, which may perhaps direct us toward a good method for examining this business. The Apostle says in one place: *Professing themselves to be wise, they became fools* <note>original Greek: φάσκοντες εἶναι σοφοὶ ἐμωράνθησαν (Romans 1:22)</note>. I shall not inquire about whom or upon what occasion this was originally spoken, and I draw no formal argument from it. I use it only because there is an appearance of great wisdom in the opinion of the skeptics; and yet, as I conceive, there is as much error and falsehood (which is "folly," as the word is often used) in this as in any other false opinion that is less popular. 

I will structure my discourse around this issue: first, to inquire what it is that makes this skepticism so popular and plausible, especially among those who pretend to have more than ordinary wisdom; and second, to lay it open to view in its true colors, so that its folly or falsehood may be visible even to people of ordinary judgment. 

First, then, regarding those who deny the existence of spirits and such things: we admit that the world is full of imposture <note>original: "imposture"; meaning deception or fraud</note>. To know this—to observe it in all trades, in all professions, and in all ranks and degrees of men—is to "know the world," and that is considered being wise. Though we call them...

<summary>The author addresses skeptics who deny the existence of spirits, stating that while he won't use the Bible to convince those who prize "reason" above all, he intends to demonstrate that their skepticism is a form of false wisdom. He proposes to examine why denying the supernatural is fashionable among the self-proclaimed wise and to expose the flaws in that logic.</summary>

<keywords>spirits, apparitions, skepticism, reason vs. faith, atheism, imposture, biblical authority, wit and gallantry, logic</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the author's argument that while many supernatural accounts are fraudulent, it is the height of wisdom to remain skeptical without being entirely dismissive. He transitions from discussing human gullibility to the history of oracles and spirits.</meta>

Jugglers <note>original: "Juglers"; here meaning street performers, tricksters, or magicians</note>; yet they deserve to be thought of as the most honest people in the world because they show their tricks openly in the streets for money, for they declare what they are. The truest jugglers are those who perform their feats—and most of them do it for money too—under the veil and reputation of holiness, sanctity (or "saintship"), religion, virtue, justice, and friendship. These are fine words used to catch men who are gullible <note>original: "of easie Belief"</note> and think that "all that glitters must be gold." 

Because of this, men who have had the reputation of being wise in the world have recommended this to us as the greatest wisdom: **NOT TO BELIEVE EASILY**. "Be sober, and remember to be skeptical" <note>original Greek: *Νᾶφε καὶ μέμνασ' ἀπιστεῖν* (Nāphe kai memnas' apistein)</note>. Epicharmus <note>a Greek philosopher and playwright famous for his pithy maxims</note> gained more credit for this one saying—and perhaps has done more good—than many who have been the authors of massive volumes. 

Now, if those things exposed to our physical senses—the proper objects of our eyes and ears—are liable to so much imposture and deceit that even the wisest can hardly know what to believe, how much more caution do we need regarding things that are so far above the senses, and in some ways contrary to them (namely, spirits), so that we are not deceived? If we consider human nature—our physical frame, the emotions of our souls, and the faculties of our minds—we will have no reason at all to wonder why most people are prone to believe and to be cheated. 

But while there is no cause to wonder, there is just as little reason to imitate them. "Happy is he who is able to know the causes of things!" <note>original Latin: *Felix qui rerum potuit cognoscere causas* (from Virgil's Georgics)</note>. A love of wonders <note>original Greek: *φιλοθαυμασία* (philothaumasia)</note>—a desire for strange things that cause amazement—is the natural inclination of the common people <note>original: "the vulgar"</note>, that is, of most men. They are born with this trait—as the wisest men who have written about human affairs have observed—and it cannot be removed except by wisdom, which is a happiness enjoyed by few. As Seneca said somewhere when speaking of human nature, "There is not only a necessity of erring, but a love of it" <note>original Latin: *Errandi, non necessitas tantum, sed amor*</note>.

There was a time when the world was largely governed by oracles. Private citizens went to them as if they were going to God, and kings and princes sent to them for advice on the most important matters. So much faith was generally placed in them that the very word "oracle" became a proverb applied to things that cannot be questioned. Yet those same ancient Pagans <note>original: "Heathens"</note> who tell us of these oracles also tell us of their vanity. Although they do not say that *all* were false and counterfeit, by admitting it of some, they give us a fair reason to suspect that the same might have been found true of the rest as well, if the same care had been taken to examine their truth. 

Again, there was a time—and that time was not many hundred years ago—when miracles were the only topic of conversation and delight for men. Ghosts and spirits were in every house, and people were so prone...

<summary>The author warns that many who claim religious or moral authority are actually "jugglers" (deceivers), and he argues that a skeptical mind is necessary because humans are naturally prone to a "love of wonders." He cites the historical example of ancient oracles and the more recent obsession with ghosts to show how easily societies can be misled by the supernatural.</summary>

men to receive what was delivered to them in that kind; that miracle-makers were much put to it, not to make their stories probable (for that was not insisted upon), but to make them wonderful enough. Indeed, some have been forced <sig>G1</sig> to complain publicly of the credulity of the people, even though those same complainers tell us much more, I dare say, than was ever true. 

As with miracles, so it is with exorcisms: how many devils and spirits have been driven out of men and women supposed to be possessed, by solemn exorcisms, to the great wonder of the beholders? Yet, upon further search and examination, these have been proved to be nothing but the artifices and subtle contrivances of men. Sentences and judgments have been passed upon such cheats when they have been discovered in most places of Europe, and these records have been published. 

But some might argue that those thought to be possessed have done strange things—things impossible, to ordinary senses, to be done by nature. It is very true, some have. But those who know what strange things may be done to the amazement

of all who are not acquainted with such mysteries—through long use and custom—will not easily wonder (so as to make a supernatural thing of it). This is true even though they see things which, to their sight and the sight of most, cannot but seem very wonderful and almost impossible. 

As for the bodily temperament of man and of his brain, it has been sufficiently proved by some recent books on that subject (**Enthusiasm** <note>original: "Enthusiasme." In the 17th century, this term referred specifically to a state of religious delusion or "possession" caused by a physical imbalance of the brain rather than divine inspiration.</note>), both by reasons from nature and by various examples. These show that a very little distemper <note>A physical or mental illness or imbalance of the "humors."</note> of the brain—scarce discernible to any but those well-versed in the study of natural causes—is enough to represent spirits, angels, and devils, or sights and stories of heaven and hell to the fancy <note>The imagination.</note>. By this "sober" kind of madness and delirium, so little understood by the common people, many have been and are daily deceived. From these things, through the ignorance of men, strange consequences have sometimes ensued, and the peace of commonwealths has suffered not a little. 

Aristotle, in his *Meteors*, tells of one who always saw (or so he thought, at least) another man's shape before his eyes; Aristotle gives a natural reason for how this happened to him. Hippocrates, in his book *On Virginity* <note>original: "Περὶ Παρθενίων" (Peri Parthenion). A short Hippocratic treatise on the "diseases of young women."</note> (a very short discourse, but full of excellent matter), shows how some, both men and women, through natural causes, come to imagine to themselves that they see "hostile demons" <note>original: "δυσμενεῖς δαίμονας" (dysmeneis daimonas).</note>, devils, and spirits, and to be tormented in their souls, even to the point of killing themselves with their own hands. The author of the book *On the Sacred Disease* <note>original: "De Morbo Sacro." (Many are of the opinion) that it contains excellent material for the same purpose; however, I do not have the book with me at this time. Hippocrates <note>The ancient Greek physician, often called the "Father of Medicine."</note> (in the passage mentioned before) shows how many people in that situation were deceived by the priests of those times, who made them believe that their condition happened to them because of the anger of some god.

"Those who are skilled in Optics know that there is a way, through the help of hidden mirrors or lenses, to create moving shadows that appear like ghosts, causing great terror to the ignorant observer. It is said that pretended astrologers and fortune-tellers cheat many people using these sights." It is the opinion of some Jewish Rabbis that whatever ghosts or souls are raised by necromancy <note>The practice of communicating with the dead to predict the future.</note> always appear *with the body inverted* <note>original: "inverso corpore"</note>—that is, with their heads downward and feet upward. Although nothing is too strange to expect from the Rabbis—who (commonly) are as full of ridiculous ideas as ever entered the head of any resident of Bedlam <note>A famous hospital for the mentally ill in London; used here to mean a person suffering from delusions.</note>—it is my opinion that the original basis for this wild idea was an image of an object gathered through a small lens into a dark room. For indeed, objects must appear *with the body inverted* if the image is projected in a high room and the objects from which the images are gathered are lower than the glass through which they pass. The reason for this is easily demonstrated to the sight of any reasonable person.

Certainly, by this secret (which is not actually a great secret, being commonly seen and practiced among those who are at all curious about science), strange things may be performed by a "cunning man" <note>A professional practitioner of magic or folk medicine.</note> to the great amazement of those who do not know the cause. There would be no end if I should attempt to collect from various authors everything that has been invented by men, and what may be done by artifice to cheat people in matters of this nature. Let any man who is still a stranger to such things read the life of Alexander the False Prophet (or Prognosticator) written by Lucian <note>A second-century satirist known for mocking superstition.</note>, and he shall see notable examples of successful cheats and deceptions. These would be scarcely credible, were it not that the events were still fresh and famous at the time of writing, and that all historical circumstances confirm the truth of the account.

Let him who reads it judge what dull and dry fellows the mountebank-astrologers <note>term: "mountebank" - a person who deceives others, especially by selling fraudulent medicines or services.</note>, prognosticators, and fortune-tellers of these days are compared to this "noble" and renowned Alexander. Only let the reader be aware that Lucian was a professed atheist; therefore, it is no wonder if he finds Epicurus spoken of with great respect, whom all atheists and those inclined toward atheism are so obliged to honor. This exception aside, I think the story is very worthy of being known, and much more worthy to be read by all men (considering the good use that may be made of it) than many books that are daily...

<meta>This page continues the author's discussion of skepticism regarding the supernatural, moving from optical illusions and Jewish folklore to the motivations of those who deny the existence of spirits and witches.</meta>

...translated from other languages. Finally, if there actually were such things as demons and spirits that appear to people, who would they likely appear to sooner than to those who call upon them daily and devote their souls and bodies to them with terrible oaths and curses? And again, who would they appear to sooner than those who, driven by sinful curiosity, have often used every method they could find in books—such as magical circles, symbols, and incantations—and yet neither group ever saw anything?

I have said as much as I intend to say (though perhaps more could be added) to show the plausibility of this opinion in opposition to common beliefs and understandings. In this way (as I believe, for I have not intentionally omitted anything I thought important), it claims for itself the titles of wisdom and extraordinary caution, which almost all men are eager to possess.

Yet I would not want it thought that all men who hold this conclusion—that there are no spirits, and so on—act so rationally, or can provide this or any other more logical and believable explanation for what they believe. God knows there are many in the world, men of no education and limited intelligence, who can speak as confidently as the most learned. This is not because they have considered the matter or understand the foundations of either opinion, but because they know or have heard that it is the opinion of some scholars, and they hope they will be thought learned as well if they agree with them.

Furthermore, there is the typical Epicurean <note>Epicurean: A follower of the ancient Greek philosopher Epicurus. In this context, it refers to someone who prioritizes physical comfort and avoids the fear of the supernatural or divine judgment.</note> (though some have been educated), who makes it his personal motto: "Let us eat and drink" <note>original: Greek phrase omitted in OCR, likely referring to 1 Corinthians 15:32: "Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die."</note> and seeks his comfort in this world through "tranquility" <note>original: Greek phrase omitted in OCR, likely *ataraxia*, meaning freedom from disturbance</note> (their own word, which implies peace of both mind and body—a good word, but poorly applied) as his "highest good" <term>summum bonum</term> <note>original: "summum bonum"</note> or greatest happiness. It is a great relief to him when strange things happen involving witches, wizards, and the like; while some people are forced to consult others or search through books, ancient and modern, sacred and secular—all of which is barely enough to satisfy their faith, reason, or curiosity.

I say it is a great relief for him, on all such occasions, to keep his soul in a state of safe ignorance and to save his reputation (and even gain credit with some) by simply saying, "It is a fable" <term>Fabula est</term> <note>original: "Fabula est," meaning "It is a story" or "It is a myth."</note>, "I do not believe it." We will hear some of them admit as much shortly; I am not making things up about them.

I will not take it upon myself to judge a book that I have never read; I cannot even say that I have ever seen it. But because I have heard some men praise an English book written on this subject to prove that there are no witches, I will share with the reader (who may not have noticed it) the judgment of one of the most learned men England ever saw regarding that book. (I wish he had been treated more kindly in his time.) By this judgment, it may appear—if his opinion is correct, as I am very inclined to believe...

Page 8

Because of his great learning and usual caution in his judgments, <note>Dr. John Rainolds (1549–1607), a prominent English divine.</note> Dr. Rainolds observed how much some men undertake to prove based on very little evidence, and how prone others are to praise whatever favors their own cause—even to the prejudice of their better judgment, if they would only judge impartially. In those elaborate *Lectures on the Apocryphal Books* <note>original: "Prælectiones de libris Apocryphis"</note>, where he critiques certain opinions of Bodin <note>Jean Bodin (1530–1596), a French jurist and political philosopher.</note> as harmful to the Christian faith, he writes:

"Reginald Scot, our countryman," <note>original: "Reginaldus Scotus, nostras"</note> he says, "who is as mad in the opposite direction as Bodin, claims that Papists admit that demons cannot even bear to hear the name of Jehovah. He had received this idea from Bodin and attributed it to Papists in general, as if all Papists agreed on it. He goes on, and because he had noticed that certain wicked women sometimes invent stories of that kind, he concludes that everything is a fiction. This stems from his lack of skill in Logic <note>original: "Dialecticæ"</note> and other noble arts. Like one who approaches this matter with no judgment, no method, and no knowledge of the best sciences, he acts just as the poet says: *An insatiable itch for writing possesses some men* <note>original: "Tenet insatiabile quosdam Scribendi cacoëthes," a quote from Juvenal.</note>; and he reasons in exactly the same way," etc.

We have been more willing to produce this passage from the writings of that learned man because we also, in our answers, may have occasion to say something to the same purpose. We do not mean to judge that author or his book, but rather the foundation upon which he built. We shall find that foundation to be the same one used by others who deny the existence of spirits. 

But we will work methodically and take everything in order, as we proposed in the objections. First, we said the world was full of imposture. It is granted that there are impostors and impostures. But what then shall the conclusion be? That therefore there is no truth in the world, or at least none that can be reached by mortal man? Truly, many books were written in ancient times to that effect. The work of Sextus Empiricus <note>A Roman-era physician and philosopher who championed Pyrrhonism (skepticism).</note> is still in existence; it is a very learned book, it cannot be denied, and is of excellent use for understanding ancient authors, especially philosophers. I could also name some who profess to be Christians—men of great learning—who have gone very far down that path. 

However, I am sure this skeptical view will not be granted by some who are, or have been, thought to be great opponents <term>oppugners</term> of the common opinion regarding witches and spirits; I mean certain physicians and naturalists by profession. But may we not argue as plausibly against the professions they practice as they have done, or can do, against spirits and apparitions? We would be loath to make so long a digression, as we have had occasion elsewhere to say something to this purpose. Those who are curious may see what has been written by Cornelius Agrippa <note>Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa (1486–1535), a polymath known for his work on the "Vanity of Arts and Sciences."</note> (who writes at great length on this subject) about it, not to mention any others. It is not yet a full twelve months since a

<meta>This page continues the author's defense of the existence of spirits and the reliability of expert knowledge, despite the frequent disagreements found among professionals.</meta>

A friend of mine, a gentleman of high social standing, brought his wife to London (some 60 miles and more from his usual home) to seek the advice of physicians. His wife—a very virtuous and religious lady—was troubled with a weak stomach and poor digestion, which caused severe symptoms. I believe he sought the advice of no fewer than a dozen doctors from first to last; I am certain he named to me five or six of the most prominent in reputation and practice that the city provides. Not one of them agreed in their opinions, either concerning the cause of the illness or the methods to be used for a cure. Consequently, the gentleman left more dissatisfied than when he arrived. 

What he did afterward, I do not know, though I know what some men would have concluded from this. Yet for my part—because of the benefits I have received from medicine and the effects I have seen of it throughout my life, both upon myself and others on several occasions (where learned professionals, not <term>empirics</term><note>original: "Empiricks"; unlicensed or self-taught practitioners, often used as a derogatory term for "quacks."</note> have been employed)—I think myself bound to honor both the profession and all its learned, talented practitioners, even if the whole world were of another opinion. I have no doubt that the worst of Agrippa’s <note>Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa (1486–1535), a scholar who wrote a famous critique of the vanity and uncertainty of the sciences.</note> objections could easily be answered by any man of sufficient judgment and experience. 

I say, therefore, that just as it is with other things in the world, so it is with matters of spirits and apparitions: though they are subject to much error and deception, it does not follow that there is no reality of truth or certainty. Such truth is discernible to those who will take the pains to search things to the bottom—where truth is commonly found—and who are naturally endowed with enough judgment to distinguish between plausible-sounding arguments and the solid truth. 

Admittedly, this proves nothing yet. No; but I hope that removing this common objection may prepare the reader to consider what we have to say with less prejudice. That shall be our next task: what we have to say in favor of the existence of spirits, etc., before we address specific objections. In this, however, I will be no longer than I must at this time, because I will have a more suitable place to discuss it in two different treatises. One of these has been in the form of loose notes and papers for a long time and is not yet organized—namely, my *Second Part of Enthusiasm*. The other is still entirely in my head but is more ready to be published because it was conceived more recently—namely, *A Discourse of Credulity and Incredulity, in things Natural, Civil, and Divine, or Theological*. In those works, we shall encounter many cases not necessary to mention here, which will help very much to clarify this matter.

I have never read a book on that subject, nor met a person with whom I had the chance to talk, who was not able to say something from their own knowledge that confirmed my belief in these matters.

(The Epicurean Atheist) who commends Democritus, Epicurus, and Metrodorus (the most famous of that sect) for their *unshakable state of mind* <note>original Greek: ἀτενὲς καὶ ἀμετάστρεπτον καὶ ἀνένδοτον</note>, as he calls it—their fixed, irrevocable, unconquerable resolution. It is not to be wondered at, then, if we see many people—despite daily experience to the contrary—stick so close to those tenets which they have wedded themselves to with such a firm resolution from the beginning, never to leave them, whether they are right or wrong.

As for Aristotle, I confess his authority is very great with me; not because I am superstitiously addicted to any of his opinions (which I shall ever be ready to forsake when better ones are shown to me), but because (besides the judgment of all accounted wise and learned in former ages) I am convinced in my judgment that so much solid reason in all arts and sciences never issued from a mortal man known to us by his writings without supernatural illumination.

Well: Aristotle does not acknowledge spirits; he mentions them not in any place. Let it be granted. And why should it be a wonder to any man who knows the drift and purpose of Aristotle's philosophy? The truth is, Plato's writings are full of prodigies, apparitions of souls, the pains of hell and purgatory, revelations of the gods, and the like. <meta>This page continues the author's argument regarding different philosophical approaches to the supernatural. Having previously discussed the stubborn skepticism of the Epicureans, the author now contrasts them with Aristotle, who preferred natural reason but did not entirely dismiss the divine.</meta>

...sometimes, and does not desire that any man should believe him according to the literal letter of his accounts, but only in general—that something was true to that effect. Indeed, he has many divine passages, even whole treatises, that can never be sufficiently admired in their own right; but it cannot be denied that they are too full of tales for a philosopher.

Aristotle, therefore, decided upon a completely opposite path: he would deal with nothing except what had some apparent basis in nature. It was not that he specifically denied all other things, but because he did not think it was the job of a philosopher to meddle with things for which no probable reason could be given. This clearly appears in a divine passage of his from *On the Parts of Animals* <note>original Latin: *De partibus animalium*, Book 1, Chapter 5</note>, where he divides substances into eternal and incorruptible <note>original Greek: ἀΐδια καὶ ἄφθαρτα (*aidia kai aphtharta*)</note>—which are, in effect, spiritual. Even spirits that were created might be termed eternal <note>original Greek: ἀγέννητα (*agenneta*)</note>, meaning, properly, those that do not have their beginning through physical birth. We will easily grant that the creation of Angels, whether good or bad, was not known to Aristotle (though we may understand them as "Gods" or "Intelligences" <term>In Aristotelian philosophy, "Intelligences" were the spiritual beings believed to move the celestial spheres.</term>). He contrasts these with things that are mortal <note>original Greek: φθαρτά (*phtharta*)</note>. 

He continues: 

> "As for divine substances, which we honor, we can say but little of them, though we desire to, because so little of them is exposed to our senses [and reason]. Mortal things, which we are familiarly acquainted with and converse with daily, we may know if we take the pains. But we should rejoice much more in the knowledge of divine things—even if we know only a very small part—because of their excellence, than in the knowledge of these worldly things, no matter how perfect and general that knowledge may be. But the comfort we have regarding worldly things (which makes some amends) is their certainty, and the fact that they fall within the reach of the sciences."

What could be said more divinely by a man who had no divine revelation? Truly, there appears to me (if I may speak without causing offense or being misunderstood) more divinity in those words than in some books that claim to be nothing else. 

Add to this another passage of his in his *Metaphysics*, where he says that although supernatural things are clear and certain in themselves, they are not so to us, who see them only with "owls' eyes" <note>Aristotle famously remarked that our intellect is to the most divine things as the eyes of bats or owls are to the sun—blinded by the brightness.</note>. Can we say then that Aristotle denied those things he refrained from writing about simply because their natures and qualities were above human knowledge? 

Nor is it absolutely true that Aristotle never wrote about spirits and apparitions. Cicero, in his first book *On Divination* <note>original Latin: *De Divinatione*</note>, tells a long story from Aristotle about a shape or spirit that appeared in a dream to a man named Eudemus (a close friend and acquaintance of Aristotle) and foretold strange things that later happened. <meta>This page continues the discussion of ancient philosophers' views on the supernatural, specifically focusing on Aristotle's stance on divination and dreams.</meta>

...a magical ring, or perhaps two, which Excestus, King of the Phocenses <note>The Phocians, a people of ancient Greece.</note>, used to foresee future events. This account can be found among the fragments of Aristotle’s works. That Aristotle did not deny the existence of witches may be seen by the mentions he makes of them in more than one place. How much importance he placed on common report and experience—even when no logical reason could be provided—is evident in the preface to his treatise *On Divination through Sleep* <note>original: *De Divinatione per insomnia*</note>. 

In that work, he presents the dilemma: how difficult it is for a rational man to believe anything based solely on reports for which he can see no reason—or which even seem contrary to reason—such as a man foretelling through a dream what shall happen in a distant kingdom without any apparent cause. But on the other hand, he says, it is no less difficult to deny what all men, or most men, believe: namely, that such predictions actually occur. 

To say (in his own words) that such dreams come from God is most unreasonable. Aside from other objections (which those who understand his philosophy would easily grasp), it is hard to believe that God would send such visions to men who are either vicious in their lives or are "idiots" <note>In the original sense: private persons or those lacking professional knowledge; unlearned.</note> and fools—the most vile and contemptible of men—who have been observed to have such dreams more often than better and wiser men. 

So, leaving that business undecided, he proceeds to consider those prophetic dreams for which some probable reason may be given. Yet in the second chapter, he says directly that although dreams are not "sent from God" <note>original: *theopempta*</note>, they may perhaps be "divine" <note>original: *daimonia*</note>; for he acknowledges Nature itself to be "divine" <note>original: *daimonia*</note> in that sense, though not "god-like" <note>original: *theia*</note>. I will not inquire further into the meaning of these words here, as it cannot be explained briefly. It plainly appears that nothing troubled him so much (for he repeats the objection two or three times) as the idea that God should be thought to favor either wicked men or fools. I wish no worse doctrine had ever been printed or preached concerning God! 

But let it still be remembered that Aristotle knew of no Divine Word or Revelation <note>The author refers to the Christian Bible.</note>. Yet Julius Scaliger <note>original: *Jul. Scahger*; a 16th-century scholar.</note>, in his commentaries upon Hippocrates' *On Dreams* <note>original: *De Insomniis*</note>, wonders why Aristotle struggled so much with this point, and Scaliger seems to provide a reason grounded in Nature. Indeed, Scaliger says something regarding the case of fools and "idiots," but nothing (that I recall) that explains the case of wicked men as well. 

Let these things be considered, and let the reader judge how different Aristotle’s temperament was from that of the ancient or later Epicureans <note>Followers of Epicurus, who generally denied divine intervention in human affairs.</note>. This mention of Aristotle and Plato reminds me of their master, Socrates, and his "Familiar Spirit" <note>The *daimonion* of Socrates; an inner voice that warned him against certain actions.</note>. This was not a physical shape, but a voice only, by which his life and actions were frequently guided. This matter is attested by so many grave authors—some of whom lived at that very time, others shortly after—that I do not see how any man can question it. Indeed, I do not remember it ever being questioned by any Heathens or Christians of ancient times...

And although they contain many mythical <note>original: fabulous</note> elements, as one might expect from such a project, they also contain so much truth and a variety of ancient learning that I believe they deserve to be better known than they usually are. However, I am certain they cannot be understood as they ought to be through any Latin or French translation I have ever seen.

No one can doubt that he [Apollonius] did many strange things with the help of spirits, which can be judged by a careful observation of the circumstances. For example, when he was summoned before Emperor Domitian in the presence of many people, he immediately vanished and was seen a long distance away (at Puteoli, I believe) around the same time. They believed he performed his wonders by the power of God, or through a secret philosophy and knowledge of nature that was not revealed to other men. <meta>This page continues the author's discussion of the complexities and potential for deception in witchcraft trials. It moves from specific historical accounts to philosophical and medical arguments regarding the existence and treatment of supernatural phenomena.</meta>

One tells us that when the cock crows, the formal gatherings of witches are dissolved. This opinion may perhaps prove ancient enough, as we shall show elsewhere. He thinks the reason might be the crowing of the cock in the Gospel when St. Peter denied Christ. Another tells us that when witches are well beaten with a vine branch or club <note>original: *trunco vitis*</note>, they "are forced to release the wicked spells they have cast" <note>original: *Malesicia illata solvere sævillina coguntur*</note>, and lose their power to do harm, or that the bewitched person recovers. The reason for this (he thinks—and he is no ordinary man either) comes "from the mystery of the wine and the vine beloved by God, from whose mystery the Sacrament of the most Holy Blood of the Lord is daily prepared" <note>original: *ex mysterio vini and vineæ dilectæ Deo, ex cujus mysterio quotidie Sacramentum Sacrosancti Sanguinis Domini consicitur*</note>, and so on. 

But I shall find a more appropriate place to fully examine these things in one of the two treatises mentioned earlier. It cannot be denied that this whole business of witches—whether through ignorance or malice—is very liable to many mistakes and various deceptions. It is to be wished that in all such trials, some prudent theologians and learned, experienced physicians might be involved. 

However, because of these errors, some—like Wierius <note>Johann Weyer (1515–1588), a physician who argued against the persecution of witches while still believing in demons</note> and others—conclude that there are no witches or sorcerers at all. Yet even Wierius acknowledges spirits, the illusions and appearances of devils, and their mischievous operations as much as anyone, and tells strange stories about them. To deny that witches exist because of these errors is like denying the power of herbs just because a thousand false and superstitious things have been written about them in the past and continue to be written today. 

Indeed, this actually happened once in Rome, as Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder, Roman author and naturalist</note> recorded at length. Some people ascribed such power to herbs that they claimed the sun and moon were subject to them, that the dead might be raised, and armies vanquished! This was not well received by many. Finally, Asclepiades arrived. He persuaded people (who were already very willing to be convinced) that the entire medical use of herbs and medicinal plants <term>simples: medicines made from a single herb or plant</term> was a complete fraud. He argued that people were better off without them, claiming there were other ways—easier and less troublesome—to restore health and overcome diseases, which he promised to teach. He was so successful for a while that herbs were set aside, and a new course of medicine <note>original: *Physick*</note> was introduced. As I said, this gave general satisfaction for a while, because people are commonly prone to embrace new inventions. 

It is well observed by Aristotle (and I think a great part of human wisdom depends on it) that in all commendable things in the world, just as there is something true and real, there is also something counterfeit and false. "There is natural beauty," he says, "and there is artificial beauty created by painting and..."

trimming. There is a true, sound, healthy complexion, and then there is that which makes a good appearance but is not actually healthy. There is true, real gold and silver, but also many things that may be mistaken for gold and silver from a distance, or by those who judge only by outward appearances. In the city of Aix <note>anciently *Aquæ Sextiæ*, now *Aquensis Civitas*</note> in Provence (a province of France), in the year of our Lord 1611, a **Roman Catholic Priest** was tried, convicted, and condemned by the **sentence** of the **court** or **Parliament** to be burned alive for abominable practices and horrific things he committed with and through the **Devil** upon various people (some of whom were of high social standing). He had long desired and sought this; at last, the **devil** appeared to him dressed as a **gentleman**. The story is found in various books in **French** and **Latin**, and was translated (at that time, I believe) into several languages. 

I would gladly travel forty miles to meet anyone who could tell me something that might induce me to believe—or at least suspect—that there was some mistake in the details of his **sentence**. For I must confess, my reason was never more puzzled <note>original: *posed*</note> by anything of that nature I have ever read. **Gassendi** <note>Pierre Gassendi (1592–1655), a French philosopher and scientist</note>, indeed, in his biography of **Peiresc** <note>Nicolas-Claude Fabri de Peiresc (1580–1637), a French astronomer and scholar</note>, mentions something (as I recall) of **Peiresc's opinion**: that he thought some of those things the priest confessed might be attributed to imagination. That wicked **sorcerer** who was burned at **Aix** predicted before his death that some misfortune would occur at the time and place of his execution; this happened exactly as predicted, and in a very strange manner. Heinrich von Sachsen, a learned professor and practitioner of medicine in Padua, wrote a book about that horrible Polish disease which he calls <term>Plica</term> <note>original: "Plicam," referring to *Plica polonica*, a condition where hair becomes matted into a felt-like mass; it was historically believed to be caused by supernatural means or witchcraft</note>, which (to the sight) turns men's hair into snakes and serpents. Hitherto I have relied on authorities rather than arguments, partly because I thought that the shortest and clearest way for everyone’s understanding, and partly because such arguments (if any besides these we have here) as have been used against this opinion may be found fully answered in the authors I have cited. The truth is, it is a subject of such a nature that it does not admit of many arguments—especially those that pretend to be subtle reasoning. Sight, sense, and experience (upon which most human knowledge is grounded), generally approved and certain, is our best argument. 

But before I finish, I will use one argument which perhaps may prove of some force and validity, and that is: a consideration of the strange shifts, evasions, and notorious absurdities that these men are forced into. These are men who, not being able to deny the *facts of the matter* <note>original: [Greek omitted] / pragma</note> or the matter of fact, would seem to say something rather than to acknowledge spirits, devils, and witchcraft.

But because those men rely very much upon the power of imagination (which indeed is very great and does produce strange effects), I shall recommend to the sober reader who has not yet encountered him, Thomas Fienus’s learned treatise, *On the Powers of the Imagination* <note>original: De Viribus Imaginationis</note>, a very rational and philosophical discourse. <meta>This page continues the discussion of skeptics who attempt to explain away supernatural phenomena through natural, albeit extraordinary, means. It focuses on the theories of the physician Auger Ferrier and the philosophical lineage of his ideas.</meta>

His reading and knowledge of good authors show him to be a sufficiently learned man. Thuanus <note>Jacques Auguste de Thou (1553–1617), a famous French historian and statesman</note> in his *History* gives him a most ample eulogy and claims he was an intimate acquaintance of Julius Caesar Scaliger <note>A renowned Italian scholar and physician</note> and much respected by him. 

However, I doubt whether Thuanus had ever seen this book of his; it does not appear from that eulogy that he had. Well, this learned man, in his chapter *On Homeric Medicine* <note>original: "De Homerica Medicatione"</note> (as he calls it), treats of cures performed by charms and spells, by words and characters <note>term: symbols or written marks used in magic</note>, which others commonly attribute to witchcraft. 

First, as for the facts of the matter <note>original: [Greek omitted], likely referring to the phenomena themselves</note>, he does not deny them. He writes: "For it is not the act of a sane man to contradict those things which are exposed to the senses" <note>original: "Nam iis quæ sensibus exposita sunt contravenire, sani hominis non est."</note>. He thinks those who deny what is proven by such visible experience are little better than madmen. 

Yet, it seems he was one of those who did not believe, or would not believe (though he does not say so positively), in spirits, witches, and supernatural operations. What then? He plainly maintains and argues (though he quotes no Gospel for it) that such is the nature of the human soul—if one knows how to use it—that by a strong faith and confidence, it may work any miracle without a miracle. 

"But that confidence and firm persuasion," (I will provide some of his words here in case you do not have the book), "is acquired by the unlearned through the opinion they have formed about magical characters and sacred words. For the learned and those who have an understanding of reality, there is no need for external things; instead, having recognized the power of the mind, they can perform miracles through it, and so on" <note>original: "Verum confidentia illa, ac firma persuasio... comparatur indoctis animus per opinionem quam de Caracteribus and sacris verbis conceperunt. Doctis and rerum intelligentiam habentibus, nihil opus est externi, sed cognitâ vi animi, per eam miracula edere possunt and c."</note>.

And again, a little later: "The learned man, remaining consistent with himself, shall heal by a word alone" <note>original: "Doctus vero and sibi constans solo verbo sanabit."</note>. 

I do not conclude from this that Ferrerius <note>Auger Ferrier (1513–1588), a French physician and astrologer</note> was the first or only person to hold this opinion, even though he speaks as if he were and names no one else. Avicenna the Arab <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), a highly influential Persian philosopher and physician</note> was the first, as I understand it, who set this idea in motion, and some others have followed him in it. 

But since these men acknowledge the strange effects that others deny, let the sober reader judge which of the two is more likely: to grant the existence of spirits and devils, or to make the soul of every man, by nature, either a god or a devil. 

However, let men take heed how they attempt to perform miracles through their "strong faith and confidence," for that is the ready way to bring the Devil to them; that is exactly what has made many witches and sorcerers. As for that faith by which men performed miracles in the primitive times of the Church, spoken of in the Gospel and commonly called "The Faith of Miracles," that is quite another thing, which I do not need to speak of here. Regarding a strong confidence in God, even in those who are not otherwise very godly—whether it may, according to God’s original order and appointment, sometimes produce strange effects—we have already considered that.

But to conclude this part: upon due consideration of the premises, and what else I have in readiness upon the same subject (if God give me life and health), I cannot satisfy myself how any learned man, sober and rational, can entertain such an opinion (simply and seriously) that there are no devils nor spirits, and so on. But I give myself this explanation (leaving all men to their own judgments in this matter): if there be any such men, truly and really, it must be because they were first biased by some plausible ground. Afterwards, being taken up with other thoughts and employments, they are more willing to stick to their former opinion without further trouble, than to take the pains to seek further. "Most people search for the truth with little effort" <note>original: the Greek quote is from Thucydides (1.20.3): "οὕτως ἀταλαίπωρος τοῖς πολλοῖς ἡ ζήτησις τῆς ἀληθείας," meaning "So little pains do most people take in the investigation of truth."</note>, as Thucydides does very well observe. 

And when we say "a learned man," there is much ambiguity in that word. For a man may be a learned man—not to speak of the ignorance of the common people, especially in those regions where they think all learning is contained in preaching; and now in these times too, they think those are the best preachers who in very deed have the least learning, but preach by instinct and inspiration, as they call it—but a man, I say, may be a learned man, a very learned man in some one field or profession, even to excellence and admiration, who nevertheless is and may be found ignorant enough in other fields. But a generally learned man is a thing of a vast extent, and not often seen. It is a business of infinite labor, besides requiring natural talents <note>original: "Natural parts"</note> to match; without which (especially judgment), the more pains one takes, the more ignorance one sometimes gains. 

I do not aim this at any particular man or men (I call God as my witness) <note>original: "Deum testor"</note>. I would much rather submit myself to the censure of others than take it upon me to censure anyone. But the observation is of very good use, I know it, and may give much satisfaction in many cases; I have given an instance of it in Tertullian <note>An early Christian author (c. 155 – c. 220 AD) known for his extensive but sometimes controversial writings.</note> and some others elsewhere.

But yet I shall answer more particularly. 

### First, Of Miracles

It cannot be denied but the world is full of horrible impostures in that particular. Yet I believe that some supernatural things, such as cures and so on, do happen in every age for which no reason can be given, and which also for their strangeness may be called miracles. ...I am quite ready to admit that many such miracles are seen in these days. But I will not argue the case further in this place. Well, let us take miracles in the ordinary sense: I truly believe that many such things do happen in many places; but through negligence partly, and partly through disbelief, they are often not regarded or are soon forgotten. Even wiser men, sometimes, though they know or believe such things, are not very eager to tell them, lest they bring themselves into contempt with those supposedly "wise men" who would sooner laugh at anything they do not understand than take the pains to correct their ignorance or inform their judgments.

I hope I shall do no wrong to the memory of that venerable, incomparable prelate, **BISHOP ANDREWES** <note>Lancelot Andrewes (1555–1626) was a hugely influential scholar and bishop, known for his role in translating the King James Bible.</note>—who was, for sound learning and true piety while he lived, one of the greatest lights of this land—if I set down two stories which we may call miracles. The first concerns a noted (or at least by many suspected) **Witch** or **Sorceress**, whom the Devil, in a strange shape, attended (or rather waited for) at her death. The other concerns a man who, after his death, was restored to life to make confession of a horrible murder committed upon his own wife, for which he had never been suspected. The first story is as follows: **L., an old woman of London, at whose death the Devil was present** <note>original: *L. Vetula Londinensis, cui morienti Diabolus affuit*</note>.

A wonderful story which the Lord Bishop related as being most certainly known to him <note>original: *Mira Historia quam narrabat ut sibi compertissimam Dom. Episcopus*</note>. There was a certain woman, L., who was very wealthy and extremely devoted to the "curious arts" <note>original: *curiosis artibus*; a common historical term for magic or the occult.</note>. Throughout her whole life, she was dedicated to sorcery, and for that reason, she was a friend and patron to infamous women of that sort. As she lay dying, while several very grave men and women were standing by, it was noticed around the hour of death that there stood at the foot of the bed a man with a terrible face, dressed in fox skins, whom she stared at with fixed eyes, and he at her. 

The doorkeeper was asked why he had let the man in, but he denied that he had even seen him. Finally, two or three people withdrew to the window to take counsel on what to do about him. Among them was a certain Alderman <note>original: *Senator*</note> of great renown... who had twice been Lord Mayor of London <note>original: *Prætor Londinensis*</note>, as well as the father of Fulke, and others. They decided to speak to the figure and ask who he was. With this intention, they returned to their previous places by the bed. Meanwhile, L. let out a great cry, as if [giving up] her soul... <note>original: *quasi animan* [sic]; the sentence is cut off at the end of the page.</note>

The other story is as follows, from the first of August. The most Reverend Prelate, the Lord Bishop of Ely <note>original: "Dominis. Episcop. Eliensis"; referring to Lancelot Andrewes</note>, told me a wonderful thing today, which he had heard with his own ears from an eyewitness and the author of the account, and he believed it to be most true. There is a street in the city of London called **Lombard Street** <note>original: "Vicus Longobardorum"</note>. In that street is a parish and a parish house, in which there was a Priest, a man of the highest faith and well-known piety, in the year 1563. In that year, if ever there was one, the plague raged through this City of London. 

This Parish Priest, therefore, told both many others and the Lord Bishop himself that this had happened to him: He had a distinguished friend in his parish; a man who, as everyone believed, was upright and pious. This man, having been seized by the plague, called for that Priest, his friend, who attended him while he was sick and saw him dying, and did not leave him until he was dead. Only then did he return to his own home. 

Quite a few hours after his death, while the body was left for dead in his bedroom, his wife entered the same room to take a blanket or linen cloth from a chest for him <note>Greek text omitted in source</note>, as is the custom. Having entered, and while intent on her task, she heard this voice: "Who is here?" 

She was terrified and wanted to leave, but that voice was heard again: "Who is here?" 

And at last, having realized it was her husband's voice, she went up to him. "What?" she said. "Husband, are you then not dead? And we had left you laid out for dead!" 

"In truth," he replied, "I was truly dead; but it seemed good to God that my soul should return to my body. But you, wife," he said, "if you have any food prepared, give it to me, for I am hungry." 

She said she had some mutton, a chicken, and I don't know what else, but everything was uncooked, though she would prepare it shortly. 

"I cannot endure the delay," he said. "Do you have bread and cheese?" 

When she had nodded and he had asked for it to be brought, he ate while his wife watched. Then, having called for the Priest and ordered everyone present to leave the room, he told him this: 

"I," he said, "was truly dead. But my soul was ordered to return to its body so that I might reveal with my own mouth a crime committed by my hands, of which no one ever had any suspicion. For I myself killed my first wife with my own hands, with such cunning that the whole matter remained hidden." 

Then he explained the manner of the crime he had committed; and not long after, he expired and was truly dead. 

There is no necessity that anyone should make either of these accounts an Article of his Faith; yet I thought them very probable, because they were believed by such a man, and therefore I have given them a place here. 

So much for Miracles. Of **Exorcisms** we must say the same as of Miracles. The story of the "Boy of Bilson" <note>William Perry, a young boy who in 1620 faked being possessed by a demon to frame a neighbor for witchcraft.</note> is well-known. Through the wisdom and insight of the Right Reverend Father in God, Thomas Morton, Lord Bishop of Lichfield and Coventry, the boy was revealed to be an impostor. He had been intentionally set up and bribed to promote the Roman Catholic cause in the year of our Lord 1620 <note>original: "An. Dom. 1620"</note>. Most countries have provided plenty of such examples and stories, which are recorded in various languages.

Nor should it be hidden (by those who seek the truth without bias) that some, formerly called "Disciplinarians" <note>Puritans who advocated for strict church discipline and often used "miraculous" healings to prove their spiritual authority.</note>—though now better known by another name—have attempted to involve themselves in these matters, hoping to gain a great advantage for their cause. There was a famous story during Queen Elizabeth's reign—though perhaps forgotten by many now and beyond the memory of anyone living—about a Mr. D. <note>John Darrell, a controversial Puritan minister famous for performing public exorcisms.</note>, a very zealous man of that sect. He took it upon himself to cast out demons through long prayers. He and others who favored that cause maintained and asserted this very strongly, although legal examinations proved otherwise. This led to many books being written on both sides in those days. Two of these were of "higher quality" <note>original: "melioris notæ"</note>, as we say, written by Dr. H. <note>Samuel Harsnett, later Archbishop of York, who wrote skeptical accounts of both Catholic and Puritan exorcisms.</note> regarding exorcisms: one against the Catholics, the other against P. <note>Likely referring to the Puritans or specifically to the Darrell case.</note>. Yet for all this, I do not conclude that Mr. D. was guilty of any imposture <note>original: "Imposture"; meaning a deliberate deception or fraud</note>: he might have done it through ignorance, being cheated by others. I have heard he was an honest man, and died piously, and disclaimed to the very last that he did anything in that business otherwise than in good faith <note>original: "Bonâ Fide"</note>. 

I would judge charitably, even of those men who are not guilty of much charity towards others—those whose judgments and consciences will not allow them (though they are men of approved worth and piety otherwise) to say as they say, and to do as they do in all things. Be it granted, therefore, that this business of exorcisms is liable to much imposture. However, no man who has read the accounts of possessed men and women in several places—with due observation of the circumstances—will make any question of the reality. Some of these accounts, besides other persons of credit, have been attested; yes, some were even penned and published by learned physicians and naturalists who were employed to find a cure. They observed the patients' behavior and heard some of them speak strange languages; they heard simple women, while possessed, discourse on the highest points of philosophy or mathematics and the like. 

No man, I say, who is not a stranger to these things (besides what some travelers, who have no personal interest in the cause, can verify upon their own knowledge) will doubt either the real possession of various people, according to the accounts that have been made, or the Devil's speaking in them and through them when they have been exorcised—and sometimes upon mere conversation. 

And though some Protestants are of the opinion that it is not lawful or justifiable for any man to take it upon himself to exorcise on such occasions—that is (as I understand it) by way of absolute power and authority, and by superstitious ways and means, as is ordinarily done—yet where a man has a calling, such as being lawfully called to the ministry and set over a parish where anyone happens to be possessed (as indeed 

I myself have a parish—that is, a right to a parish as good as the laws of the land can give me—which has been grievously haunted for many years, though not altogether in the same way, to the undoing of many there; but I must not come near it, nor have the benefit of the law to recover my right, though I was never told why), and if he finds himself zealously moved, yet without presumption, I would not despair. I believe his prayers, along with other acts of devotion and the assistance of others of the same calling, might prove effective before God. But it is still presupposed, as most expedient and necessary, that the opinion and decision of one or more learned and conscientious physicians be obtained in the case, and their presence also required in all proceedings.

Sometimes princes, sometimes private men—just as they now use religion, preaching, praying, fasting, masses, and processions (as most princes and states do in all places)—made good use of them for their own ends and made them speak what they themselves had prompted. But one might just as easily argue that because some have been so freely acknowledged to have been created by secret agreement <note>original: "compact"</note> and bribery <note>original: "subornation"</note>, it is more likely that those which were never suspected should be true. 

We read of many such cases in Herodotus <note>A famous Greek historian often called the "Father of History."</note>: of one which was devised by fraud, but there we also read that when it became known (even though care had been taken to hide it), the chief schemer <note>original: "Contriver"</note>, a powerful man, was banished—or avoided a worse fate by a voluntary exile—and the sacred virgin or prophetess was deposed. 

But not to dwell on specific details, which would take too long, it is most certain—and it will clearly appear to those who are well-read in ancient authors and histories—that all pagans <note>original: "Heathens"</note>, generally the wisest and most learned among them, especially those who lived when oracles were most common, really believed them to be what they claimed to be. That they were indeed genuine for the most part (assuming that their gods were actually devils or evil spirits) can be made evident by many accounts and other strong proofs. Neither was it ever doubted or denied by ancient Christians (though it was always granted and presupposed that, as in all worldly things, much fraud did intervene and intermingle); I am sure this was acknowledged by most, if not all. But I have spoken of them elsewhere already, and therefore I will be brief here. 

Our last objection was: if there are devils and spirits, why do they not appear to those who do everything they can to invite them, whether through continual curses or profane curiosity?

It is one thing to require a reason for things that are purely natural, and another for those that happen by a purely secret Providence. <meta>This page continues the editor’s introduction to the life and works of Dr. John Dee, transitioning from his general reputation to the specific goals of this publication.</meta>

...have it reprinted here immediately following this Preface. His *Mathematical Preface* to Euclid is, I think, the one among all his published writings that has been most noticed in England, and it added much to the value and praise of that edition of Euclid. He was a married man and had several children, as will appear by this account <note>original: "Relation"</note>; he was a great traveler and lived to a great age. 

But as I said before, I do not intend to provide a general account of his life to others, as I am still unfamiliar with it myself. Regarding this account that I am presenting, I will provide the details, and I hope nothing will be missing for that purpose. I have set four goals for myself to that end: 

First, to somewhat confirm the truth and sincerity of this entire account. 
Secondly, to answer some objections that might be raised against parts of it. 
Thirdly, to clarify certain passages and satisfy the reader regarding the completeness or imperfections of the book, as well as the original manuscript. 
Fourthly and lastly, to show the many good uses that a serious Christian can make of all this.

**I.** It seems that Dr. Dee began to have the reputation of a magician <note>original: "Conjurer"</note> early on. He complains about this very bitterly in that Preface to Euclid I just mentioned, near the end of it, yet he also calls himself "an old, worn-out mathematician." For my part, I still have some doubts whether he could ever truly be called a magician. I am very confident that he did not consider himself one, but rather a devoted worshiper of God and a very sincere, open Christian. How this can be reconciled with the truth of this account will be considered later. 

Regarding the truth and sincerity of the account, I hope no one will so deeply misunderstand us as to think we intend to vouch for what is printed here against any suspicion of forgery—as if someone, taking advantage of Dr. Dee's name and his reputation as a magician, could be suspected of dreaming up and inventing these things in his own head to deceive the world. I would be sorry for my name to appear in any way on a book liable to such suspicion. Furthermore, the very name and reputation of that highly and deservedly prized library from which this is claimed to be taken is enough (for reasonable and informed people) to prevent the absurdity of such a mistake. Besides, the original manuscript itself, all written in Dr. Dee's own handwriting, is kept and preserved there. 

By "truth and sincerity," I mean not only Dr. Dee’s honesty in reporting what he himself believed, but also the reality of the things he speaks of in his account. His only (but great and dreadful) error was that he mistook false, lying spirits for angels of light—the Devil of Hell (as we commonly call him) for the God of Heaven. For the...

Regarding the truth, sincerity, and reality of the account in this sense, I shall first appeal to the book itself. I know it is the habit of many book-buyers (I will not say that I have never done it myself) to turn five or six pages; if they happen upon something that pleases their fancy, they decide the book is a good book. Once they have bought it, they feel compelled to think so because they have paid for it. On the other hand, if they land on something that does not please them (which may happen even in the best works), they are just as ready to condemn and throw it away. It is very possible that some such buyer, coming across this book and finding certain passages here and there where odd, strange things appear—things that seem ridiculous or incredible to ordinary common sense—may be ready to judge the whole work accordingly. 

But despite this, I will first appeal to the book itself, though with this request to the reader: that he will have the patience to read at least one-fourth of the book in order before he passes judgment. If by that time he is not convinced, he has my permission to give it up. It is not that the rest of the book, even to the end, does not help very well to confirm the truth and reality of the whole story; rather, it is because I believe there is so much in any fourth part—if read diligently and with due consideration—that I despair of gaining the agreement of anyone who is not convinced by it. 

For my part, the book was first shared with me by that most worthy gentleman who is very diligent in purchasing and obtaining such records and historical documents <note>original: "Monuments"</note> as may benefit the truth of God (all truth is of God) and the honor of this land. In this, he follows the example of his noble ancestor, known to all the learned as far as Europe extends by his very name: Sir Robert Cotton. 

<margin>Sir Thomas Cotton, Knight and Baronet.</margin>

I read it quickly at first because I was soon convinced within myself that it could be no counterfeit or imaginary business, and I was very desirous to see the end, as far as the book went. I took notes of the most remarkable passages as they appeared to me. Truly, I was so much confirmed in my first opinion by my second reading that I shall not be afraid to declare that I never gave more credit to any human history of former times. Readers will likely agree with me. Nevertheless, to help those who do not trust their own judgment, let us see what can be said. First, I would suggest that those who want further proof read Dr. Dee in his previously mentioned Preface. There, he pleads his own case to clear himself of that serious crime and accusation of being a "conjurer" <note>original: "Conjurer"; in this period, a conjurer was someone believed to summon demons or spirits through magic.</note>. I must admit that the Preface was written long before his communication with spirits; yet it is helpful to know what opinion he then held regarding those who deal with devils and evil spirits. 

But after he became acquainted and deeply involved with them, and had prepared several of these books (or others on the same subject) containing their various conferences and communications—showing exactly how they appeared—please observe the confidence with which he approached the greatest and wisest leaders in Europe. He often approached Queen Elizabeth and her Council, as many parts of this account show, but specifically in his letter to Sir Francis Walsingham, the Secretary of State. That he did the same with King James and his Council can be gathered from the (admittedly incomplete) records of 1607 included in this account. 

He also went to the Emperor Rudolf II, to Stephen, King of Poland, and various other princes and their representatives—the wisest and most learned men their courts could provide at the time. The details of all these meetings and transactions are recorded very precisely in the book. Indeed, his confidence was so great that, had the <term>Apostolic Nuncio</term> <note>original: "Nuncius Apostolicus"; a high-ranking diplomatic representative of the Pope.</note> not appeared against him at the Emperor's court by order of the Pope, it seems he was determined to go to Rome as well. He did not doubt that he could justify himself and his actions to the Pope and his Cardinals. 

In all these approaches and petitions, he was always ready to share everything with those who would treat the matters with the respect he felt they deserved. He was even willing—which is quite notable—to admit those he deemed worthy and capable of helping the cause into this "Mystical Society." He <term>actually</term> <note>original: "de facto"</note> did this for several people in various places: Albertus Alasco, the Prince Palatine of Poland; Puccius, a learned man; and Prince Rosenberg in Germany, who were members of the Society for a long time. Others, like Stephen, King of Poland, were admitted to specific "Actions" <note>In Dee’s journals, an "Action" refers to a specific session or ritual of spirit communication.</note> for a short time. 

We will easily admit (as has been discussed in detail elsewhere) that a disturbed mind may see or hear strange things and believe in them with total confidence as if they were real, even though they are merely fantasies without any actual sound or apparition. But the visions and apparitions that Dr. Dee describes here are of an entirely different nature; even though it is possible the Devil might represent several of these things to the imagination internally...
