<meta>This page continues Méric Casaubon's examination of Dr. John Dee’s character, specifically addressing the difficult question of why a seemingly pious man would be abandoned by God to the influence of evil spirits.</meta>

...did not live long. Secondly, an objection may be raised—or at least a point of hesitation—as to how God would permit a man like Dr. Dee to be so deluded and abused. By these papers, he seems to have been a good, innocent, and even pious man, and a sincere Christian (excepting his delusion and its effects). Why would God allow him to be so tortured in his soul and harassed in his body for such a long time by evil spirits, despite his frequent, earnest, and zealous prayers and appeals to God? According to his own account, this continued even to his dying day, for all we know.

Truly, if one considers the whole conduct of this business from beginning to end, according to this true and faithful account presented to us (and I believe I can call it that with confidence), one sees how this poor man was shamefully and grossly delayed, deluded, and picked on without cause from time to time. He was constantly lured <note>original: "toled on"; enticed or drawn forward, like the tolling of a bell</note> by various shows and appearances, yet always frustrated and rebuffed. When we look at his many pangs and agonies, and his sad condition after so many years of toil, travel, drudgery, and earnest expectation—at the very last, as appears by the spiritual "Actions" and apparitions of the year 1607—I do not know whether he should be an object of more horror or compassion. Certainly, he deserves both in great measure from anyone who has a sense of humanity or who recognizes human frailty in the examples of others; and likewise, from anyone who respects intellectual talent and worth, which this man possessed in a high degree. 

It is true that he also had joys and comforts, though they were imaginary and delusory. I have no doubt that he enjoyed these, that they sustained his spirit and often made him appear outwardly cheerful. These are the same kinds of feelings that the "Saints" (as they call themselves) and schismatics <note>original: "Schismaticks"; those who promote divisions or splits within the Church</note> of both past and present times have always been very prone to boast about, convincing themselves that these feelings are the work of God's blessed Spirit. But even in these joys and comforts—which were merely the fruits and fancies of his deluded soul, as is the case with many others who have a disturbed brain—is he not an object of great compassion to anyone who is both sober-minded and charitable? 

If this was indeed his situation, what shall we say? If nothing else, I believe the following ought to satisfy any rational, sober, and humble person: we must say that it is not within human power to explain all of God’s judgments. We have no reason to complain simply because we do not understand them, or because they often seem contrary to the judgment of human reason. It is against all reason as well as religion to believe that a creature so naturally inferior to God as man is should see everything as He sees it and think as He thinks—and consequently, to judge and decide on all things exactly as God judges and decides.

<summary>Casaubon addresses the theological problem of why a pious man like Dee was permitted to be deluded by demons, concluding that human reason cannot fully comprehend God's mysterious judgments.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Méric Casaubon's analysis of Dr. John Dee’s character. Having previously discussed the possibility of Dee being a pious man deceived by spirits, Casaubon now explores the specific sins—namely pride and curiosity—that may have led to his downfall.</meta>

Therefore, the Apostle—not without reason—would have all private judgments deferred until that time when the hearts of all men shall be laid open and all hidden things and secret counsels revealed. (As for public judgments intended to maintain peace and order among men, that is a different matter.) 

But we have enough to say in this case without relying on that. For if pride and curiosity were enough to ruin <note>original: "undoe"</note> our first parent <note>Adam</note>, and through him all of mankind—even when they were otherwise innocent and in possession of Paradise—should we wonder if it had the same outcome for Dr. Dee? This is true even though he otherwise appears to us to have been innocent and well-qualified. 

That this was his specific case and error, I will appeal to his own confession (though he makes it his boast) in more than one of his letters or addresses. In these, he professes that for several years he had been an earnest petitioner <note>original: "suter"; someone who petitions or requests</note> to God in prayer for wisdom. That is, as he explains it himself, so that he might understand the secrets of Nature that had not been revealed to men until now. He professes that his purpose was to glorify God—and his own deceitful heart may have suggested this to him—but the actual goal was certainly that he himself might become a famous man in the world. He hoped to be admired, or even nearly adored everywhere, as he was sure would happen if he achieved his desire. 

And what do we think prompted such a desire and the hope of obtaining it, other than the high opinion he had of himself as an extraordinary man—both in his talents <note>original: "parts"</note> and in his favor with God? Regardless of how great he actually was, in addition to his spiritual pride (a sin as great as any in the eyes of God), his praying for such a thing with such persistent urgency <note>original: "importunity"</note> was a great tempting of God that deserved the most severe judgment. 

If he had indeed been a petitioner to God for the kind of wisdom described by the prophet Jeremiah (9:23–24): "Let not the wise man glory in his wisdom... but let him who glories, glory in this," etc.; and if he had sought the knowledge commanded by our Savior (John 17:3): "And this is eternal life, that they may know you," etc.; and as the blessed Apostle said (1 Corinthians 2:2): "For I determined not to know anything [among you except Jesus Christ and him crucified]," he would have had good justification for his prayers. It is very likely that God would have granted his request, as far as it concerned his own salvation and eternal happiness. 

Furthermore, it is lawful—and even appropriate—for a man to pray for God’s blessing upon his work, and for a sufficient amount of intelligence and ability so that he may do well in his calling <note>original: "vocation"</note> and glorify God. But for a man to aspire to such prominence above others through extraordinary means—such as the imaginary <term>Philosopher's Stone</term> <note>A legendary substance sought by alchemists, believed to turn base metals into gold and provide the elixir of life</note> and the like—and to involve God through earnest pleas in his ambitious and extravagant desires is a different matter. Since God has said of himself that He resists the proud but gives grace to the humble, such an act must be (if considered carefully) so great a provocation that I begin to doubt whether it is charitable to pity a man who suffered so much...

<summary>Méric Casaubon argues that Dr. John Dee’s downfall was caused by spiritual pride and an obsessive curiosity to uncover hidden secrets of nature. He suggests that Dee's persistent prayers for extraordinary wisdom were a "tempting of God" rather than an act of true piety.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Méric Casaubon's critique of spiritual pride and intellectual overreach. He uses the example of Dr. John Dee's obsessive prayers for secret wisdom to illustrate how even seemingly pious desires can be rooted in vanity and a lack of humility before God's established order.</meta>

...justly and deservedly. I do not know but that it is as lawful for any man born in obscurity to pray for a kingdom, for a common soldier to pray for the strength to encounter thousands, or for an ordinary maid to pray that she may become the fairest of women.

In all these cases, we grant that it is possible to glorify God—if it were proper for us to dictate to God how He should be glorified while neglecting those means He has already appointed, and if we could be certain that in claiming to seek God's glory, we were not actually seeking our own. I wish that our great "undertakers" <note>original: "undertakers"; here meaning those who take on ambitious, experimental, or visionary projects</note> and reformers of the arts and sciences (who think themselves so wise) would seriously consider this. I mean especially those who take it upon themselves to make all men wise and of one mind, and to reconcile all doubts and difficulties in religion and other fields—in short, to make Truth embraced by all men. 

If these men were to tell us that if they had been in charge of creating the world and ordering all things from the beginning (and I think there are some in the world who have said little less), they would have made a different sort of arrangement than God did, we would perhaps wonder what could give a mortal man such incredible confidence. But given the current condition of the world and of human nature—or, to speak as a Christian, given the Fall of Adam and its consequences, such as the curse of God and so on—the idea of making all men wise, like-minded, good, and religious without an infinite, omnipotent power (the kind that could create a world from nothing) is absurd. Can any sober and wise man hear such a thing—hear it with patience—when he already considers it impossible, even strange, that castles should be built in the air or the heavens battered with great cannons? 

And yet such books are read and even highly valued by some men. In my judgment, those who boast of such things are to be pitied if their boasting is caused by a mental imbalance <note>original: "distemper"</note>, as I believe it is for some. But if they are being clever and calculating <note>original: "politick"</note> just to get credit and money (as I believe some are), then their confidence is a strong proof that there are many people in the world who are not very wise. 

But to return to Dr. Dee: it could be further proved by examples that even men of extraordinary holiness and self-denial <note>original: "mortification"</note> in the eyes of others—men so secluded from the world and its vanities that they seemed to converse with God alone for many years—have nevertheless fallen into delusions and temptations because of pride and a high opinion of their own talents <note>original: "parts"</note> and favor with God. These delusions might not be exactly the same as Dee's, but they are no less strange and dreadful. Church history <note>original: "Ecclesiastical Story"</note> and other similar books provide many such examples. I do not have them at hand right now, but I believe I have said enough on this point. But of his...

<meta>This page continues the author's critique of religious enthusiasm and the dangers of unguided, spontaneous prayer, specifically targeting the belief in personal inspiration over established liturgy.</meta>

Something should also be observed regarding prayer. His "spirits" tell him somewhere that he had the "Gift of Prayer." Truly, I believe he had it, as it is commonly called: that is, he could express himself very fluently and earnestly in prayer, and he did so often to his own great satisfaction. Let no man wonder at this; I have shown elsewhere that some who have been very wicked—even some who died for blasphemy, with blasphemy in their mouths until their last breath—have possessed this gift in great measure and done much mischief with it. This is no discredit to prayer, any more than it is to the best things in the world (and what is better or more heavenly than prayer when well used?) if they are abused. It is commonly observed that the corruption of the best things is the most dangerous. 

What bred those destructive heretics who troubled the world for so long, and could not be suppressed except by absolute destruction, but long, affected prayers and "enthusiasms" <note>original: "Enthusiasms"; in this context, it refers to the belief that one is directly possessed or inspired by a divine spirit, often leading to erratic behavior</note>? For this reason, they were called <term>Euchites</term> or <term>Messalians</term> <note>original: "Euchites" or "Messaliani"; both terms mean "those who pray," referring to a 4th-century sect that believed constant prayer was the only way to expel demons</note>, which is to say, "The Prayers." 

As for that point of inward joy and self-satisfaction which some schismatics <note>those who promote division or separation within the church</note> and wicked men find in themselves during their prayers—which ignorant, deluded people think is proof of the Holy Spirit—it is a certainty. It is a mystery of nature that has (may I say it without bragging) been brought to light, or at least fully discovered in recent years by myself: "That not only the inward heat of mental thought (where there is any vigor) but also the music of spoken words is able to cause this feeling." 

Indeed, it is a point that deserves to be well considered, especially in these times. For when young boys and illiterate men are turned loose to exercise themselves in this "gift" (as they call it)—and the number is likely to increase now that catechizing <note>the formal instruction of Christians using a series of questions and answers</note> is so neglected—and when by long practice they have attained some readiness and fluency, it causes an inward lightness and excitement. Or, perhaps, it creates something that resembles spiritual sorrow and remorse. They immediately think themselves inspired, and so they become "Saints" before they even know what it means to be Christians. 

And if they can pray by inspiration, why not preach also? This is how Anabaptism <note>a radical religious movement often associated by 17th-century writers with social disorder and the rejection of infant baptism</note> creeps in by degrees, which will be the ruin of all religion and civil government wherever it prevails. I believe that this foolish, fond conceit of "Inspiration" has been the cause of much mischief, including that horrid sacrilege—or profanation, I should call it (and I hope I may do so without offense, for it is not done by any public authority that I know of)—the casting out and banishing of **THE LORD'S PRAYER** from many private houses and churches. I think Christ never received a greater insult than this.

I am not so uncharitable as to believe that it is done in direct opposition to Christ by any real Christians; rather, I believe it is done out of a furious zeal by many who are against set prayers <note>The author is likely referring to Puritans or radical sectarians who preferred spontaneous "extempore" prayer over the prescribed liturgy of the Book of Common Prayer</note>. Certainly, as the Lord’s Prayer is a prayer of most incredible comfort to those who use it devoutly and upon good grounds (by which I mean a good foundation of religion and sound faith), so I believe that set prayers in general are of more importance to the settling of peace in the Commonwealth than many men realize. But let this pass as my opinion; I am sure there are worse opinions that circulate freely.

Again, a man may wonder (and I do not know whether an objection may be made of it) that Dr. Dee—though he was at first deluded (to which his own pride and presumption exposed him) as many have been—remained so even later. In the process of time, when he found himself so deluded and shuffled about; when Edward Kelley used such pregnant <note>original: "pregnant"; meaning compelling or highly significant</note> arguments to him (as he did more than once) to persuade him that they were evil spirits appearing to them; nay, even when he had found by certain experience that his spirits had told him many lies and foretold many things concerning Princes and Kingdoms—very particularly limited with circumstances of time—which did not come to pass at all when the time expired; yet for all this, he dared to pawn his soul for them, insisting they were good spirits, and continued in his confidence (so far as our account goes) to the last.

I answer: such is the power of this kind of spiritual delusion. It so possesses those whom it has once taken hold of that they seldom, if ever, recover themselves. In the days of Martin Luther (a great and zealous reformer of religion, but one who would have detested as the worst of infidels those who have misused the Lord’s Prayer as some have done in our days, as appears by what he says of it in more than one place), there lived one Michael Stiselius <note>Michael Stifel (1487–1567), a German monk and mathematician who became a follower of Luther but famously miscalculated the date of the Apocalypse</note>. Applying certain passages of the Apocalypse <note>The Book of Revelation</note> to himself, he took it upon himself to prophesy. He had foretold that in the year of the Lord 1533, before the 29th of September, the end of the world and Christ’s coming to Judgment would occur. He showed so much confidence that some write that Luther himself was somewhat startled at first. But when that day passed, he came a second time to Luther with new calculations and had digested the whole business into 22 articles. The effect of these was to demonstrate that the end of the world would be in the following October. But by now Luther thought he had seen enough evidence and gave him so little credit that (though he loved the man) he silenced him for a time. Our apocalyptic prophet took this very poorly and wondered much at Luther's lack of faith.

But why speak of individual men? Consider the Anabaptists <note>original: "Anadaptists"; a radical religious group during the Reformation</note> in general. Over a hundred years ago, they troubled Germany greatly, and it cost many thousands their lives. They roamed up and down the land. No sooner were they destroyed in one place than they sprang up in another (as long as that season lasted). Their claims were the same everywhere: "revelations" and "the Spirit," the wickedness of princes and magistrates, and the claim that Jesus Christ was to be set up on his throne. Well, eventually they were destroyed in most places. Stories about them have been written in all languages and read everywhere, as has their miserable end. 

Yet can all this prevent them from starting up again in the same shape and form as before? Whenever there is an opportunity provided by a confused and chaotic <note>original: "confounded"</note> government, they reappear with the same excuses and the same Scriptures—which are, for all the world to see, miserably distorted and abused—to provoke riots and rebellions <note>original: "tumults and seditions"</note> everywhere. Such is the wretchedness of a man who has once left the right path of reason and sobriety.

Some things happened at times (such as his danger and preservation near Gravesend when he first left the kingdom, as related here) very strangely. Such was the misfortune of his misplaced zeal that he interpreted everything that happened according to his desires as an act of Divine Providence.

First, I answer that this is a very weak objection. We know by the constant experience of both present and past ages that those who are the greatest and richest are not commonly the best of men. The greatest harm is to themselves, for they are deluded—and indeed, many are bankrupted sooner or later—and to a few unwise people whom they cheat just as they themselves have been cheated.

I have no doubt that had Dr. Dee <note>John Dee (1527–1608/9), a famous mathematician, astronomer, and occultist who claimed to communicate with angels</note> gone to Constantinople and been received there with respect, his spirits would have shown themselves to be as good "Mohammedans" <note>original: "Mahometans"; an archaic term for Muslims</note> as they were good Roman Catholics or Protestants elsewhere.

We have a very charming tale somewhere (I would call it a curious observation if I thought it were true) concerning the nature of the serpent or adder, beautifully expressed, about how she trains her young ones to go out into the world so they may fend for themselves. Twenty days, as I recall, are spent in that work. Now, whether it is actually so, I cannot say for certain, but I suspect it. It is not in Aristotle <note>The ancient Greek philosopher whose biological works were authoritative for centuries</note>, and I looked in Aldrovandus <note>Ulisse Aldrovandi (1522–1605), a renowned Italian naturalist and author of massive encyclopedias on natural history</note> and could not find it. But whether it is true or not, let no one wonder; for this was the manner of preaching formerly (and perhaps still is in some places) that was in great demand among monks and friars. 

They would create stories of men or beasts as they saw fit, as best served their imaginations—as clever and witty as they could. No one required the story to have any basis in truth as long as the moral was good. If the Devil has done so here, it was not through ignorance (for he is too good a naturalist; and I believe there is something even in nature, though we do not know it, why in both sacred and secular <note>original: "prophane"</note> history, spirits and serpents are so often joined together) regarding what is true and real. But as has been said, it served his purpose, and that is enough.

But I have something else to say regarding this case of devils and spirits in general, which I think is very significant and may perhaps provide satisfaction in some cases where nothing else can. We talk of spirits and read of spirits often, but I think the best of us know very little about them, their nature, or their differences. How then can it be expected that we should resolve all doubts? And though I think it is not much that any man ever knew or rightly understood—or can understand while he is a mortal man—in this business; yet my opinion is (though I know it is much denied and opposed) that the ancient **Platonic Philosophers** of later times understood much more than most Christians. I do not write this because I think, or would have others think, that anyone is a worse Christian for being ignorant of these things; rather, in my opinion, a man is a much better Christian if he does not regard or desire such knowledge. 

For my part, although I must acknowledge that some doubts in my mind induced me to look into many books until I was satisfied—which I otherwise would never have done—yet I profess to believe that so little can be known by man on this subject, and it is so subject to illusion, that I think no study is more vain and foolish. I would not go three steps out of my doors (beyond what I did to satisfy my mind in matters of faith, if any such doubt arose) to know as much as the profoundest Platonic, or philosopher, or even the greatest magician of them all ever knew. 

Certainly, he is but a weak Christian who cannot find a better way to spend his time, especially when so many high mysteries are proposed to us in Christ through his Gospel, which are of such great consequence. Those who have any hope, through faith in Christ and a godly life, to be admitted one day into the presence of God and to see him "face to face" as God has promised—will they hazard so glorious a hope by prying through unseasonable, unprofitable curiosity into the nature of these subordinate spirits, which God has forbidden? 

But because it concerns religion in general that we believe in spirits, and when objections are made that cannot be answered, many people are offended and **Atheists** are ready to take advantage of it; I say, it should be no wonder to any sober and rational person if we cannot resolve all doubts. ...commonly called) are either angels of heaven or devils of hell. I know of no scripture for this, nor any decree of a general council that I can recall—at this time, at least—and as long as that is the case, I do not think I am bound to accept it against clear reason. As for the idea <note>original: "conceit"</note> that all evil spirits or devils are confined in hell, I believe the learned Mr. Mede <note>Joseph Mede (1586–1638), an influential English scholar and theologian who argued that some demons inhabit the air rather than a subterranean hell</note> has addressed that in some of his works and sufficiently disproved it.

The very word "spirit" is a term of great ambiguity. We usually understand it to mean substances that are entirely immaterial. It is well known that many of the early Church Fathers did not allow for any such purely immaterial beings except for God himself. We tend to think that having no visible body and being purely immaterial are one and the same; God knows how many stages <note>original: "degrees"</note> there may be between these two states, but we cannot know it, nor does it affect our salvation—for which we have reason to praise God.

But if it were true that all spirits are either devils or angels, what should we make of those found in mines, about which the learned Agricola <note>Georgius Agricola (1494–1555), a German scholar known as the "father of mineralogy," who wrote about spirits encountered by miners</note> has written? Or what of those who have been called "kobalos" <note>original Greek: κοβάλους (kobalous); mischievous spirits or sprites from which the word "goblin" is derived</note> since time immemorial? These spirits live in private houses, around old walls and piles of wood; they are otherwise harmless but very thievish. They are so common and well-known in some countries that a person might as well doubt if there are horses in England simply because there are none in some parts of the world (I believe they were not found in all of America until some were carried there).

Nor can I believe that those spirits who enjoy nothing but harmless pranks and playfulness—the kind known in all ages, like those that used to shave the hair of Pliny the Younger's <note>Plinius Secundus (61–113 AD), a Roman lawyer and author</note> servants during the night, as he himself relates in his letters (and he is a very reliable man, I am sure)—I cannot believe, I say, that such spirits have any connection to either heaven or hell. We could provide more details, but we do not wish to dwell on it at this time; and there is still something else to be said.

I could give the reader a view of them all here put together, but it would be superfluous.

<meta>This page continues the editor's preface, discussing the provenance and physical condition of Dr. John Dee’s spiritual diaries before their publication.</meta>

On September 3, 1584 (which was a Monday), Dr. Dee first appeared before the Emperor Rudolf <note>Rudolf II, Holy Roman Emperor, known for his interest in the occult</note>, having been presented by honorable persons and expected by the monarch. Among other things, he told the Emperor that for the past two and a half years, God’s holy Angels had been informing him of various matters. Our book, or the first recorded action here, begins on May 28, 1583. According to this calculation, the first apparition must have begun more than a year and three months before that date. We are, therefore, missing the account of those first fifteen months. I cannot say how much material that might amount to in bulk; nor will I guarantee that everything is perfectly preserved from May 28, 1583, to April 4, 1587, although for the most part, the coherence is consistent enough up to that time. 

But from that date until March 20, 1607, there is a vast <term>chasma</term> <note>original: "chasma or hiatus"; a large gap or void</note> of no less than twenty years. I cannot say for certain how this happened, but my guess is this: some years after Dr. Dee’s death, Sir Robert Cotton bought his library (or what remained of it), along with his <term>Magical Table</term> <note>A consecrated table used by Dee and his scryer, Edward Kelley, for spirit communication</note> (which I will discuss later) and the original manuscript written in Dee's own hand, of which this book is a copy. 

The book had been buried in the earth—for how many years or months, I do not know. Even though it was carefully kept after it was found, it had retained so much moisture from the earth that it began to moulder and perish some years ago. When Sir Thomas Cotton (mentioned previously) observed this, he paid the costs to have it transcribed before it was too late. Now, nearly fifty years have passed since this original came into Sir Robert’s possession. It is very likely that if any more had been heard of during all that time, Sir Robert—or his son and heir, Sir Thomas—would have heard of it and acquired it as readily as anyone else. 

Because nothing more has been heard of in all this time, it is more than probable that no more exists, neither in England nor, I think, anywhere else. Perhaps the rest perished, at least in part, even while the Doctor was alive. We shall find in this account that a good portion of his "holy books" were burned, but (strangely enough) a great part of them were recovered and restored with the help of spirits. Or it may be that since his death, the rest rotted in the earth because the place where they were hidden was unknown. 

If, as is probable, no more of the text survives, we may consider what we have here to be "perfect" in the sense that it is all that can be obtained. Some people—as is the nature of many, if not most, to desire what cannot be had rather than be content with what is available—might greatly lament the loss of the rest. They might be less pleased with this volume because so much is missing (though we do not know for certain if it is much or little). I would ask them to consider this: even if there had been twice or thrice as much more...

<meta>This page continues the editor's preface, discussing the decision-making process behind publishing these specific records of spiritual communication and the moral lessons to be drawn from them.</meta>

As all this material came to light, what should have been done with it? For my part, regarding what is set out here (which is all we had), I thought it would be best to have it all printed. Although it is somewhat long, it is a very extraordinary thing and of great consequence for many good purposes and uses. Yet we did consider the matter carefully, and perhaps others would have thought that a smaller amount would have served the purpose. But I hope more people will be of my mind; there are few actions that do not afford something extraordinary or, in some respect or another, something observable and useful. Regardless, I am confident that if all the records had survived (supposing the rest would have been much more voluminous), none or very few people would have thought it appropriate to print everything. And if it had once come to a contraction or abridgment, perhaps much less than this would have had to suffice. 

Every man is free to think as he pleases; for my part, all things considered, I find no great lack in the missing parts. If I were pressed, I cannot say for certain that I wish more of it still existed. Yet it gives me great contentment—and I hope there is no blasphemy or superstition in saying this, if I ascribe it to Providence—that after that long intermission, or gap <note>original: "hiatus"</note>, we still have the very last actions. By these, it might appear—after many goodly shows and promises, so much hope and expectation, so many prayers, and so many thanksgivings and humiliations—what the end result is of dealing with devils and using unlawful means to achieve ambitious, unjustifiable desires. 

Besides, whether the missing portion is large or small, I am confident we have the most important parts preserved here. Specifically, we have an exact account of his addresses and dealings with the Emperor and other great men and princes in the seventh and following divisions. We also have that sad story of their promiscuous copulation <note>This refers to the "cross-matching" or wife-swapping commanded by the spirits to Dee and Kelley</note>, performed under the persuasion of obedience to God, which is related very particularly in the twelfth division. In that account, the cunning and malice of evil spirits—leading people away from God while they most pretend to be following God and godliness—is clearly shown. So too is the danger of affected singularity and seeking eminence (the first ground of all this mischief), as well as spiritual pride and self-conceit. These are eminently set out for every man’s observation, provided he is not already too far committed to such principles (as too many are in these times). 

But nevertheless, I must acknowledge that there is one part of the story missing which I believe most readers will greatly desire. And how he acquired it, and indeed what became of it, would be worth knowing if it were at all possible. All that we are able to say of it is this: it was a stone in which, and out of which—by persons who were qualified for it and admitted to see it—all shapes and figures mentioned in every "Action" <note>original: "Action"; this refers to the spiritual sessions or séances conducted by John Dee and Edward Kelley</note> were seen, and voices were heard. The form of it was round, as appears by some coarse representations of it in the margins, such as on pages 395, 399. b, and 413. b; and it seems to have been of a significant size. It seems it was most like a crystal, as it is sometimes called, as on page 80, "Having inspected the crystal" <note>original: "Inspecto Chrystallo"</note>, and page 177. b, "nothing visible appeared in the Sacred Crystal except the visible form of the crystal itself" <note>original: "nihil visibile apparuit in Chrystallo Sacrato, præter ipsius crystalli visibili formam"</note>. Everyone knows by common experience that smooth things are best suited for reflections, such as mirrors and the like; but ordinarily only those things are represented which stand opposite and are visible in their substance. 

But it is a secret of Magic (which happily may be grounded, at least in part, upon some natural reason unknown to us) to represent objects that are not externally visible in smooth things. And Roger Bacon (also known as Bacun) in a manuscript titled *On the Sayings and Deeds of False Mathematicians and Demons* <note>original: "De dictis et factis falsorum Mathematicorum et Dæmonum"; note that "Mathematician" in this period often referred to astrologers or occultists</note>, shared with me by my learned and much-esteemed friend, Dr. Windett, a Professor of Physics in London, has an observation to that purpose in these words: 

"To these mathematicians, complete in their wickedness, demons appear sensibly in human form and other various forms, and they say and do many wonderful things for them as God permits. Sometimes they appear imaginarily, such as in the fingernail of a virgin boy who has been enchanted; and in basins and swords, and in the shoulder-blade of a ram consecrated according to their manner, and in other polished things: and demons show them everything they ask, as God permits. Therefore, boys thus looking into polished things see imaginarily things that were stolen, to what place they have been carried, and which persons carried them away; and so of many other things, the appearing demons show all these things to them for the worse." <note>original Latin: "Hiis Mathematicis in malitia suâ completis apparent Dæmones sencibilitur in forma humanâ et aliis formis variis, et dicunt et faciunt multa eis mirabilia secundum quod Deus permittit. Aliquando apparent imaginarie ut in ungue pueri virginis carminati; and in pelvibus and ensibus, and in spathulâ arietis secundum modum eorum consecratis, and in cæteris rebus politis : and Dæmones ostendunt eis omnia quæ petunt, secundum quod Deua permittit. Unde pueri sic inspicientes res politas vident imaginarie res furtive acceptas and ad quem locum deportatæ sunt, and quæ personæ asportaverunt ; and sic de aliis, multis, dæmones apparentes omnia hæc illis pejus ostendunt."</note>

Joachim Camerarius (that worthy man mentioned before) in his introduction to Plutarch’s *On Oracles* <note>original: "De Oraculis"</note>, etc., has a strange story on the credit of a friend of his, whom he much respected (as he himself claims) for his piety and wisdom. The boy would first see a man in it, dressed in such-and-such a way, and afterwards whatever he desired. No one other than a boy with those qualifications could see any—

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the ritual tools and manuscripts of John Dee, specifically focusing on the identity of the "show-stone" and the physical "Holy Table" used during his spiritual conferences.</meta>

The Sanctified Stone, the usual Show-stone <note>original: "Shew-stone"; a crystal or mirror used for scrying or spirit communication</note>, and the Holy-stone might be thought of as separate and different objects, but I understand them to be the same. This is the account we can provide regarding this primary Holy-stone. To address the lack of information <note>original: "supply the defect"</note> about how it was first brought to him, the reader may find some satisfaction by reading the detailed account of how it was taken away and restored, which was noted previously on another occasion.

Besides this stone (or stones), various other sacred objects are mentioned that belonged to this simulated <note>original: "personated"; likely meaning a sanctuary represented in physical form or acting as a stage for spiritual entities</note> sanctuary. Nothing is mentioned more frequently than curtains—or a "curtain" or "veil," as it is sometimes called. One might think at first, perhaps, that this was a physical object on the outside, but it will be found otherwise. It was seen within the stone and appeared in different forms and colors, as those who read this will quickly discover.

Next to these, the Holy Table is of primary importance <note>original: "chiefly considerable"</note>. Its arrangement was assigned to Dr. Dee, though he did not dare to take it upon himself until he had authorization from his spiritual teachers. This table, which may well be called "magical," is preserved and can be seen in Sir Thomas Cotton's library (where we obtained the rest of these records). With his permission, it is represented here in an engraving <note>original: "brass Cut"</note>. Mention is made of it, as I understand it, where Dr. Dee asks his teachers whether the table—specifically the central cross that unites the four principal parts—is made correctly or not. You may read more about it; it is also called the Table of the League, the Table of the Covenant, or the *Table of the Covenant* <note>original: "mensa foederis"</note> in some places. Its pedestal is mentioned in two or three places, as well as a very intricate <note>original: "curious"</note> frame belonging to it, which can still be seen in the same library.

However, I do not know what to make of the passage where neither "Nalu" <note>Likely a spiritual name or a specific term from Dee's angelic language</note> nor the Table appeared, and the "round table" or "globe" also did not appear. I believe this must refer to something that had appeared previously in the stone. A reader who is inquisitive enough may soon find the answer by reading carefully; I was not willing to spend too much time on it.

But a major matter remains for us to explain to the reader: there were many tables or diagrams <note>original: "Schemes"</note> at the end of the book. These contained letters (a, b, c, etc.) arranged into small squares, with an inscription over each table in that unknown script <note>original: "Character"; referring to the Enochian alphabet</note> mentioned before, with the pronunciation expressed in common letters. One example is included here at the end of the preface as a sample. The rest were omitted because it was judged unnecessary to include them, unless the goal was simply to increase the price of the printed book. First, although Dr. Dee himself went to great trouble to understand the mystery behind them and was given great hope from time to time that he would reap the benefit of his laborious work and long patience (a point he complains about in several places), it never led to anything. And if he gained nothing from them to benefit himself, what hope did we have? Furthermore, we may judge these tables, and this entire mystery of—

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the nature of secret writing and the potential involvement of spirits in the works of certain scholars.</meta>

Letters, based on what we have seen in others of the same kind. Johannes Trithemius <note>Johannes Trithemius (1462–1516) was a German abbot and polymath known for his work on cryptography and his reputation for practicing magic.</note> was a man who was supposed by most to have dealt with spirits for a long time, and to have been instructed by them in some of those secrets that he claims to possess in his books. I know some have thought him innocent, or at least have attempted to justify him. Some people take up such causes to show off their wit; they think they will be considered much wiser than other men if they contradict received opinions, though their vanity and strong conceit of their own abilities are their chief, if not only, motivation. 

The learned and judicious Master Vossius <note>Gerardus Vossius (1577–1649), a Dutch classical scholar and theologian.</note> has shown himself very willing to think the best of him and his books; yet he gives up at last and rather concludes the contrary. Those who dare defend Apollonius <note>Apollonius of Tyana, a 1st-century Greek philosopher often compared to Jesus and accused of being a sorcerer.</note>—the greatest upholder of paganism <note>original: "Ethnicism"</note> that ever lived, and accounted by most heathens as either a god or a magician—need not hesitate at anything of this kind. 

But let him be whatever any man wants him to be; we are speaking of Trithemius. He published his *Polygraphy* <note>A work on cryptography published in 1518.</note> during his lifetime, dedicated to the Emperor of that time. He tells the world of the greatest wonders to be performed by it that were ever heard of: all wisdom and arts, all languages, eloquence, and everything else are included in it. But I never heard of any man who could make anything of it, or reaped any benefit of any kind. I think this is the reason that his *Steganography* <note>Trithemius's most famous work, which disguised a system of cryptography as a book of black magic.</note>—mentioned and promised in this first work—was not printed until so long after his death. It was expected that it would have shed some light on the first book; but neither from that one, nor from this later one, could anything ever be made by any man, as far as I have heard. 

I have good reason for what I say. For besides what others have acknowledged, I find the learned Vigenère <note>Blaise de Vigenère (1523–1596), a French diplomat and cryptographer.</note>—who in his old age had become very interested in the Kabbalah <note>original: "Cabalistical"; referring to Jewish mysticism or secret occult knowledge.</note> (or perhaps had a natural disposition toward it, though he was otherwise very learned)—was as well-versed in that book as any man before him. He plainly professes that he could make nothing of it. And truly, if he could not—having bestowed so much time and effort in those unprofitable studies—I see little hope that anyone else should. 

It would make a man almost hate learning to see what foolishness <note>original: "dotage"</note> even the most learned are subject to. I could bless those who know but little, provided they knew that it is but little they know and were humble. But it commonly happens otherwise: those who know but little think that little to be much and are very proud of it; whereas much knowledge (or to speak properly, more knowledge), if well used, has this advantage: it makes men most sensible of their own ignorance. <meta>This page continues the editor's preface, discussing the relationship between Dr. Dee and the Polish nobleman Albert Laski, as well as the physical condition of the original manuscripts.</meta>

A stranger to the book might wonder: the business is that Dr. Dee had lately entered into a great alliance and confederacy with Albert Laski (or *a Lasco*, rather), a prominent man from Poland <note>original: "Polonia"</note>. You have already read what Camden <note>William Camden (1551–1623), a famous historian and antiquary</note> says of him regarding his arrival in England at this very time and his departure, which agrees very well with the dates recorded here. It seems that although he was nobly born and held great dignity, his thoughts aspired much higher. Though he was not a rich man for someone of his rank and quality, he expected such great things from Dr. Dee and his spirits that he could find enough money to supply their needs when necessary. 

The spirits were very glad for this opportunity and did what they could to encourage him according to his temperament. At that very time, they were engaged in deliberations that depended heavily on Albert Laski and his good opinion. Among other things, his pedigree—which would surely please a vain man—was taken into consideration. I do not guarantee that everything said there exactly matches the truth, nor do I have the leisure at this time to take the pains to examine it. We must never look further into things delivered by such spirits than to see if they were relevant (whether true or false) to their goal and the current occasion. 

Besides, it is very possible (and I desire the reader to take good notice of this) that both here and elsewhere the transcribers may have made mistakes. Sometimes they could not read the text and were forced to leave blanks (though seldom to any significant harm to the meaning). They were dealing with an original manuscript that was—and still can be seen—as defaced and worm-eaten as this one is, written (as we have said) by Dr. Dee himself. In addition to the authenticity of the original copy written by Dr. Dee, the reader should know that the original letters shown here are all, or mostly, still preserved and can be seen in Sir Thomas Cotton’s library.

IV. I have now come to the last of the four things I promised: to show the various good uses that may be made of this book, which were the primary reasons for publishing it. I had proposed this order to myself, but since a great part of this topic arose during other matters, it has already been covered in the previous discourse; therefore, little is left to be done. However, I will sum them up and present them together so that every reader may have them ready and in view for their better use. 

The first use is against atheists and those who do not believe that there are any devils or spirits. I confess we have argued this quite extensively at the beginning of this discourse or preface, and I hope some may receive adequate satisfaction from what we have said. <meta>This page continues the author's theological and philosophical reflection on the spiritual dangers presented in the preceding narrative of Dr. John Dee’s angelic conversations.</meta>

Authority—which would be irrelevant to use against Atheists—I do not know what could be more convincing than this tragic story, which has been so precisely, particularly, and faithfully delivered. Truly, others must see further than I do if they can find a rational answer or opposition to this. This is a significant point and a major foundation of Religion; but this is not all. For if there are indeed spirits so wicked and malicious, so diligent and industrious in deluding men and doing mischief (which is their ultimate goal), all of which is fully shown in this account; then it must certainly follow that there is a great, over-ruling Power that takes care of the Earth and its inhabitants. This Power especially protects those who adore Him and worship Him with true affection and sincerity. 

For without this over-ruling Power, what a miserable world we would have! What person could be so sober or innocent that they could enjoy themselves at any time with any comfort or security? Furthermore, what person can read this tragic story and be so confident in their own wisdom or innocence that they do not, in some degree, reflect upon themselves? Such a reader will be moved to praise God that—despite many provocations of various kinds (such as damnable curiosity, open profaneness, frequent oaths, curses, perjuries, a scandalous life, and the like)—God has been pleased to protect and preserve them from the force and violence of such enemies of mankind. 

I said before that the greatest confusion has often followed from small beginnings. This is very true, as seen particularly in the case of Bacchus <note>The Roman god of wine and ritual madness; the author views his cult as a historical example of demonic deception.</note> many ages ago, and in the case of Muhammad <note>original: "Mahomet"</note> later on. These were two notable, wicked enthusiasts <note>In this period, "enthusiast" meant someone who falsely claimed to be directly inspired by God or a spirit.</note> through whom evil spirits, by God’s permission, brought great changes to governments and committed much mischief and villainy among men and women, as we shall show more extensively elsewhere. 

By carefully considering all the circumstances—especially their confident and repeated addresses to and attempts upon so many great men in power and authority—I am strongly of the opinion that these spirits had as high hopes for Dr. Dee as they ever had for Bacchus or Muhammad. But God was not pleased at that time to permit their malice and cunning to prevail. And I think, if we consider it well, we have reason to praise God for it. England might have been overrun with Anabaptism <note>A radical religious movement that the author associates with social chaos and the rejection of established church and state authority.</note> long before now—and when I say Anabaptism, I mean Anabaptism confirmed and in full power, not merely as it appears in its initial claims. God be thanked that it was not so then, and "God keep us from it still" is, I hope, the prayer of all truly sober and religious people. 

Indeed, I see no reason why the wisdom and prudence of Her Majesty’s Council <note>The Privy Council of Queen Elizabeth I.</note> at that time, in opposing Dr. Dee’s frequent petitions and solicitations, should not (under God) receive some part of our thanks and acknowledgment. The case of one Mr. Nicholas was proposed to the Assembly for consideration. He was accustomed to sneak into private houses under the pretense of praying and would gather small congregations. This business was disliked by the pastors for several reasons:

"On Friday, July 18, 1589, when it was reported to the assembly regarding Master Nicholas—who was working his way into various houses secretly, so that small groups sometimes used to gather—the pastors disapproved of the practice. It was then narrated by Beza that on the preceding Saturday, while that very fierce battle was being fought before our eyes, he was asked by a humble woman, 'What, Mr. Beza, do you wish to say prayers here?' He replied, 'Not at all. Do you think,' he said, 'that I am only watching these things with my eyes, and not pouring out prayers in my soul to God, the Best and Greatest?' Indeed, prayer is a holy thing of the highest order, which one should not approach without meditation; for those who think it is an easy thing to compose prayers well are mistaken. At the same time, we must take care that we do not unknowingly open a path to any superstition."

Finally, all people may take warning from this example of how they remove themselves from the protection of Almighty God—either by presumptuous, unlawful wishes and desires, or by seeking help not only directly from devils (which <term>Dr. Dee</term><note>John Dee (1527–1608/9) was a famous mathematician, astronomer, and advisor to Elizabeth I who became deeply involved in "angel magic" and alchemy.</note> certainly never did, but rather hated the very thought of it in his heart), but from those who are closely related to devils. These include witches, wizards, conjurers, <term>astrologers</term><note>The author views astrology as a gateway to demonic influence rather than a science.</note> (those who take it upon themselves to predict human events), fortune-tellers, and the like. This also includes all books on those subjects, which I suspect were a major cause of Dr. Dee’s delusion. 

It is certain enough that people are commonly cheated by such individuals. Anyone who is not a complete fool would be careful how they deal with them and would avoid them simply to avoid being seen as a fool. But those who are wise should avoid them even more if they are capable of doing more than just cheating; for the more they can actually do, the more we know they have the devil in them. Wretched people! They will not and dare not trust God, who is the only fountain of...

### Postscript

POSTSCRIPT. Since this Preface was written and almost printed, I was shown a book entitled *Theatrum Chemicum Britannicum* <note>original: "British Chemical Theater," a famous collection of English alchemical literature published in 1652</note>, etc., by Elias Ashmole, Esq. In some annotations at the end of that book, there is an account concerning Dr. Dee and Edward Kelley (there styled Sir Edward Kelley) taken from a diary of Dr. Dee’s, all written in his own hand. Just as I do not question Mr. Ashmole's honesty in this matter, I also have little doubt that Dr. Dee’s own handwriting will be found to agree in all matters of fact both in that book and this one, if anyone takes the trouble to compare them. It may be that the reader will receive further satisfaction regarding certain details through Ashmole's work, which is the reason I mention the book here, having only recently learned of it. 

I do not interfere with Ashmole's judgment concerning either Dr. Dee or Kelley; perhaps, had he seen what is presented here in this volume, he would have held a different opinion on some things. There is enough here, I am sure, to satisfy any man who is not already biased or otherwise committed to his own private goals. As for those reports concerning Kelley (some of which also involve Dr. Dee) that Ashmole mentions, while I believe that he heard such things, I must truly profess that I have encountered far different accounts. In my judgment—and based on the account given to us here by Dr. Dee—these other reports are much more probable. 

Specifically, I have heard that Kelley was imprisoned by the Emperor <note>Rudolf II, Holy Roman Emperor</note> for a notable <term>chemical cheat</term> <note>original: "Chymical cheat"; a fraudulent claim of being able to transmute base metals into gold</note> that he had performed on him. Although the details were fully related to me, I will not venture to repeat them lest I make a mistake in some technical terms or minor circumstances of the event. 

Let the reader judge by the account Dr. Dee (who knew him best) gives throughout this entire book regarding this man Kelley, whether Weaver’s story in his *Funeral Monuments* (pages 45–46) is not much more probable than anything said by others in Kelley's defense or praise. Weaver describes damnable <term>necromancy</term> <note>the practice of communicating with the dead or using black magic</note> and other diabolical conjurations practiced by Kelley in Lancashire. This indeed makes Doctor Dee’s case altogether inexcusable: that believing and knowing the man to be such a person, he would still associate with him and expect good to come from his services. It shows that the Doctor’s faith and his intellect (through God’s just judgment, as we have said) were so much in the power and...

# Dr. Dee's Apology

<page-num>58</page-num>

->**Dr. Dee’s Apology, Sent to the Archbishop of CANTERBURY, 1594/95.**<-
->OR, A letter containing a very brief apologetic discourse <note>original: "Discourse Apogeticall." In this context, an "apology" is a formal defense of one's positions or actions, rather than an expression of regret.</note>, with a plain demonstration and fervent protestation for the lawful, sincere, very faithful, and Christian course of the philosophical <note>In the 16th century, "philosophy" encompassed the study of the natural world, including what we now call science, as well as mathematics, alchemy, and metaphysics.</note> studies and exercises of a certain studious gentleman: a longtime servant to Her most Excellent Royal Majesty.<-

**To the most Reverend Father in God, the Lord Archbishop of Canterbury, Primate and Metropolitan of all England, one of Her Majesty’s most Honorable Privy Council: my exceptionally good Lord.**

Most humbly and heartily I crave your Grace’s pardon if I cause any offense by sending or presenting such a simple discourse as this to your Grace's hand. However, in the opinion of some wise and discreet friends <note>original: "nay friends," likely an OCR error for "my friends."</note>, it is thought not irrelevant to my most urgent petitions currently in progress (before Her most Excellent Royal Majesty, your Lordship’s good Grace, and other Right Honorable Lords of Her Majesty’s Privy Council). It is thought helpful to make some part of my former studies and scholarly exercises—practiced and continued for these past forty-six years—known and revealed first to your Grace and the other Right Honorable Lords of Her Majesty’s Privy Council.

And secondly, to afterwards permit the same to be viewed by the public. This is not so much to stop the mouths and eventually halt the impudent attempts of the rash and malicious inventors and creators of most untrue, foolish, and wicked reports and fables concerning my aforementioned scholarly exercises—pursued with my great (even incredible) efforts, travels, cares, and costs in the search for and learning of true philosophy. Rather, it is to certify and satisfy the godly and impartial Christian listener or reader that, by their own judgment (after considering and examining this significant portion of the details of my attached philosophical studies and exercises), they will or may be sufficiently informed and persuaded that I have labored wonderfully to find, follow, use, and frequent the true, straight, and most narrow path that leads all true, devout, zealous, faithful, and constant Christian...

And this book of mine <gloss>G1</gloss>, by God's help and favor, shall be dedicated to her most Excellent Royal Majesty [Queen Elizabeth I]. This treatise contains three books:

1. The first titled: *On the Horizon: A Mathematical and Physical Book* <gloss>G2</gloss> <note>original: "De Horizonte: liber Mathematicus and Physicus"</note>.
2. The second: *On Eternity: A Theological, Metaphysical, and Mathematical Book* <note>original: "De Æternitate: liber Theologicus, Metaphysicus and Mathematicus"</note>.
3. The third: *On the Horizon of Eternity: A Theological, Mathematical, and Sacred-Technical Book* <gloss>G3</gloss> <note>original: "De Horizonte Æternitatis: liber Theologicus, Mathematicus, and Hierotechnicus"</note>.

Truly, I have great cause to praise and thank God for your Grace’s <note>Likely referring to Archbishop John Whitgift, who acted as a mediator for Dee</note> very charitable treatment of me: both in many other points and also in your favorable yielding to—and even announcing—the proper means for carrying out her Sacred Majesty’s most gracious and bountiful intention, resolution, and very royal beginning to restore and give to me (her long-time faithful servant) some proper maintenance. This would allow me to lead the rest of my old days in some peace and comfort, with the ability to hire several fast, neat, and accurate <gloss>G4</gloss> <term>Orthographical: here meaning writers who use correct spelling and clear, standard handwriting</term> scribes to assist me. Furthermore, I require these scribes for the fast, neat, and accurate copying of other ancient authors’ good and rare works in Greek or Latin <gloss>G5</gloss>, which by God’s Providence have been preserved from the looting of my library and all my movable goods here [at Mortlake], etc., in the year 1583 <note>In 1583, while Dee was traveling in Europe, a mob attacked his home and library at Mortlake, destroying or stealing many of his instruments and books</note>. ## A fervent PROTESTATION.

Eternal salvation in the Lord. <note>original Latin: "Domino sempiternam [salutem]"</note> Sincerely weighing the circumstances and merits of the men studying in our University, we believe that only those whom we know to have earned it through their learning, character, and integrity should be honored with our testimonial, so that they might obtain this benefit from us. The Almighty and most merciful God, the Father; for the sake of his only Son (our Redeemer) Jesus Christ: by his holy Spirit, so direct, bless, and prosper all my studies and philosophical exercises (indeed, all my thoughts, words, and deeds) from now on, even to the very moment of my departing from this world, that I may clearly and abundantly be found, and undoubtedly acknowledged by the wise and just, to have been a zealous and faithful student in the School of Truth, and a long-standing graduate in the School of Charity: to the honor and glory of the same God Almighty, and to the sound comfort and confirmation of those who faithfully love and fear his Divine Majesty and sincerely continue in the labor of doing good on earth—when, while, to whom, and as they may. Amen. ### THE CONTENTS OF THE SECOND PART. 
**Part II, Action I, page 1.**

Content resembling a sermon: Doctor Dee (having zeal but lacking true understanding <note>original: *not according to knowledge*; a biblical reference to Romans 10:2</note>) was wonderfully moved by it. Prince Rosenberg’s expectation of money was answered and then evaded with great cunning <note>original: *subtilty*</note> by using examples from Scripture—such as Abraham, David, and Solomon. It discusses the precious powder he possessed and how and when it should be used. It also mentions judgments to be carried out against several powerful figures (which certainly would have happened if they had succeeded) by Prince Rosenberg, acting as if on God’s behalf.

Edward Kelley’s wife is barren, and the reasons why. He is very weary of his role <note>original: *office* as a spirit medium</note> and is scolded for it. Another person (Arthur, Doctor Dee's son) is to be put in his place. Furthermore, Kelley's portion of the precious powder will be taken from him if he does not repent.

¶ **II** page 4. Arthur is first presented and prepared through prayer, etc. He begins his duties <note>original: *Office*</note> and sees various things in the stone, such as lions and men, but he hears nothing.

¶ **III** page 5. Arthur acts again as before. Three exercises in

...one day. **IV** page 7. Arthur <note>John Dee’s young son, whom he attempted to use as a medium</note> acts as medium again, as before: in two more exercises.

**V** page 8. Edward Kelley resumes his office <note>his role as the primary "scryer" or medium</note> again: he sees and hears as before. This involves the "Anabaptist" doctrine <note>referring to radical 16th-century religious sects often accused of promoting communal property and polygamy</note> of committing adultery for God’s sake, etc. Regarding some specific words here, see the *Errata* <note>list of printing errors</note>.

**VI** page 9. Here the spirits begin to show themselves in their true likeness, teaching the "doctrines of devils." Yet they still speak in the name of God (just as their instruments do in various places today). Doctor Dee and Edward Kelley are exhorted—indeed, commanded—to have their wives in common <note>this refers to "cross-matching," a notorious episode where the spirits commanded Dee and Kelley to share their wives sexually</note>. The case is argued stiffly and eagerly on both sides.

Other strange doctrines of devils (noted and rejected in the Preface) are mentioned, such as murder being condemned by the laws of men but approved by God. Saint Paul is impiously slandered. Great promises are made in exchange for obedience. 

**The Powder** <note>the alchemical "Projection Powder" used in attempts to transmute base metals into gold</note>. The Pope is accursed here, yet elsewhere in the text, Catholicism <note>original: "Popery"</note> is justified. Kelley is scandalized; Doctor Dee is in great agony. Some secrets of distillation <note>an alchemical process</note> are revealed by the spirits. The Powder is mentioned again, and how Edward Kelley obtained it. 

Predictions regarding England (all of which proved false and foolish). Edward Kelley’s fidelity is suspected. There are Cabalistic <note>original: "Cabalistical"; referring to Jewish mystical traditions involving the secret meanings of letters and numbers</note> mysteries of letters and numbers, which were not well understood by Doctor Dee, even though he was much helped by his spirits. But at last, he feels joy (in spirit, as he is persuaded) and resolves to obey.

Doctor Dee, Edward Kelley, and their two wives: their senses, apprehensions, and resolutions concerning this newly enjoined doctrine of "promiscuous copulation" <note>sharing partners</note>. This is expressed in the form of a **Covenant** (as they called it) with God. It is first shown here, and afterwards (on page 20) completed and signed by the parties. 

It includes a most wicked clause, or conclusion, of dreadful curses <note>original: "imprecations"</note> upon anyone who should ever come to know of it or reveal it. However, it is much to the glory of God and true religion that such "mysteries of Hell and darkness" should come to light, so that they may be abhorred by all men, and so that others may be warned by such sad examples not to hunt after new doctrines and pretended inspirations and revelations.

On page 17, Edward Kelley makes a declaration of his dislike of these spiritual actions in general from the beginning, and his opposition when the occasion arose. He expresses his dislike of this new doctrine in particular as being contrary to the revealed Will of God. He is eventually satisfied to some measure, and thereupon shows his readiness to obey. But when the women profess their dislike and hesitation <note>original: "demurre"</note>, he resolves to give up all further dealing with the spirits.

**VII** page 19. Apparitions occur. The "chief Stone" <note>the crystal "shew-stone" used for scrying</note> is carried away by spirits in their sight. More exhortations and arguments are given to force compliance with this new doctrine. A miracle is offered for further confirmation.

**VIII** page 21. Another apparition appears (upon request) to confirm them in their purpose of obedience.

**IX** page 22. Yet another apparition for the same purpose. The **Covenant** is torn by Kelley.

All from here to the end shows us only the sad and lamentable catastrophe of this long delusion. Kelley is no longer heard of now, yet the spirits still appear in the same shapes as before.

Year of our Lord 1607 (Julian Style <note>the "Old Style" calendar used in England at the time</note>), March 20. By this time, Doctor Dee had become a very old man. If he were sixty years old <note>original Latin: "Sexagenarius"</note> (as he is described in Puccius's letter in 1586), he must be eighty or older by this time. We need not take the word so precisely, but however old he was then, he must be very old now, as I said before.

### THE CONTENTS OF THE THIRD PART

**Part III. Action I** page 32. Raphael (or a spirit pretending to be him) is sent to Doctor Dee to comfort him; for, besides old age, he is much afflicted with poverty and sickness.

**II** page 33. The same Raphael speaks of a certain treasure hidden somewhere underground (as was supposed). Doctor Dee’s questions are eluded rather than really answered. There are more delays and promises of "wonderful wisdom," etc., as before.

**III** Ibid. A voice is sent to Doctor Dee while he is (as it seems) alone.

**IV** page 34. Raphael...

...again: an entity who, with many attractive pretenses and very forceful rhetoric (at least to someone like Doctor Dee), delivers a message to him. This message concerns a journey to a far country, to be undertaken by Dee in his current miserable state of health and poverty, despite his advanced age and present illness. The message describes the danger of his disobedience and the reward for his obedience; the Philosopher's Stone <note>original: "Philosophers Stone"; a legendary substance capable of turning base metals into gold and granting eternal life</note>, and so on. Doctor Dee is willing to go. (What rare faith—or rather, what an extraordinary but well-deserved delusion!) There is mention of Salisbury and his devils, if the devil can be believed at all.

¶ page 36. Certain cases and questions are proposed, or are to be proposed. It seems Doctor Dee, at this time, took it upon himself to act as a "Cunning-man" <note>a professional practitioner of folk magic, often sought for finding lost goods or predicting the future</note>. His necessity, which was great, might have pushed him to try all means to survive, but I think he was too honest to actually prosper by such a trade.

### Page 77

**V** page 39. The same spirit, Raphael. Some questions are resolved (though I doubt how truthfully) concerning hidden treasure. The journey is hurried along. There is a reference to the History of Tobias <note>a book from the Apocrypha where the Archangel Raphael guides the young Tobias on a journey</note>. 

**VI** page 40. Raphael appears in the Stone <note>the "shew-stone" or crystal used for scrying</note>. The Jewel and the Powder <note>likely the alchemical "red powder" or projection powder used in attempts to transmute metals</note> are in Doctor Dee's possession, but they are not yet of any use to him. He expresses his thankfulness (good man that he was). 

**VII** page 41. Raphael appears again in the Stone. The journey is discussed. There are great promises of wisdom and other things. Mention is made of Doctor Dee's enemies at Court. Money intended for Doctor Dee by the Emperor <note>Rudolf II, the Holy Roman Emperor, who had been a patron of Dee and Kelley</note> (also mentioned on page 38) was hindered. Certain cases concerning himself and others are answered at his request. 

**VIII** page 43. Raphael: Various questions and cases are answered by him. One John Pontoys <note>John Pontois, a merchant and loyal friend who stayed with Dee until the end of his life</note> is very ambitious to serve Doctor Dee during these apparitions.

¶ These records end here in our narrative, and probably ended with his life; or at least—even though his spirits had promised him (page 34) many more years of life—they ended not long before his death. I cannot yet learn the exact time of his death, but by all reports, it was around this time and certainly occurred in England. Though his sin was very great (as shown in the Preface), because of his simple and sincere intentions toward God, it may charitably be hoped that God was merciful enough to let him recognize his error and repent of it before he died.

¶ page 46. That which follows here is certainly intended to be part of that "Holy Language" <note>often called "Enochian" by modern scholars</note> which Adam is said to have spoken in Paradise (Part I, pages 64, 92), and through which great wonders might be performed. I have neither the faith nor the curiosity to inquire into it any further; nor, I think, will any sober man. Instead of any other endorsement, the reader may consider how concerned the Devil has been when he saw that his plots were not likely to succeed because God opposed them. (The reader should also consider the judgment of the late Archbishop of Armagh <note>James Ussher (1581–1656), a famous scholar and prelate</note>, so famous everywhere for his piety and learning, as mentioned on the first page of the Preface, as well as the judgment of various others who read the manuscript book and wished it to be printed.)

# Errata
## Page 78

**ERRATA:** Many errors will be found in the book. A good portion of these proceed (aside from ordinary typographical mistakes, which occur even where the best care is used) from the lack of correction in the copy <note>original: "Coty," likely an OCR error for "Copy"</note>. This lack of correction might have happened partly through the illegibility of the original manuscript itself in many places, and partly from mistakes in the said original even where it was most legible. The cause of these mistakes and errors in writing may be found in Part I, page 159, line 20, etc. Besides what is said there, it may probably be gathered from Part II, page 27, line 43, and page 23, line 20, and other similar places, that Edward Kelley, for the most part, when he reported voices and speeches to Doctor Dee (especially those of some length), did not know what he was saying himself, and so might the more easily make mistakes. 

A good part of the Greek in Part I, page 27, was misreported and mistaken, as is shown in the Preface, page..., and I believe it was never thoroughly understood by Doctor Dee himself. It cannot, therefore, be expected otherwise than that there should be many faults in the writing. For these, I would not have the innocent (meaning the printers and correctors) bear more blame than is their share. 

Yet, however many there are, most are such (excepting those places where the original was very faulty) as may easily be corrected by an ordinary reader who is familiar with books of all kinds. Or, if not so easily corrected, they are at least such as will not rob the reader of the main sense and matter. Some few passages here and there, perhaps, will be found where even a reasonable scholar may be challenged. For example, in Part II, page 9, line 11: *alias vobismet ipsis disimperuis* <note>original Latin; a corrupted phrase</note>, which certainly must be read as *alas vobismet, ipsis disruperitis* <note>original: "alas vobismet, ipsis disruperitis"; meaning "Alas for yourselves, you will break [the wings] yourselves"</note>. There is a manifest (and relevant) allusion in these words to that allegorical "wing-breeding" or "wing-bearing" <note>original: [Greek omitted] likely referring to *pterophuia*</note> of the soul, which is so famous in the books of the philosophers, especially the Platonists. That very expression is to be found in Plato (or works commonly ascribed to him), not only...

<meta>This page transitions from the introductory corrections by Meric Casaubon into the primary records of John Dee's spiritual actions. It documents a conversation between Dee and Edward Kelley regarding the Polish nobleman Albertus Laski, followed by the appearance of a spirit named Madini.</meta>

28. 1583. <margin>G1 Δ. This symbol represents Dr. Dee; E.K. is Edward Kelley. See the Preface.</margin> <margin>G2 Albertus Laski</margin> Δ. As John Dee and Edward Kelley sat talking about the noble Polish nobleman Albertus Laski and the great honor he has obtained here with us, his great popularity among all ranks of people—both those who see him and those who only hear of him—and again, how much I was beholden to God that Laski’s heart should so fervently favor me, and that he strives so much to suppress and defeat the malice and envy of my countrymen against me (thereby helping me win or recover my reputation so that I might do God better service hereafter), and so on. 

Suddenly, there seemed to come out of my oratory <note>original: "Oratory"; a small private room for prayer</note> a spiritual creature, like a pretty girl of seven or nine years of age. Her hair was rolled up in the front and hung down very long behind. She wore a gown of serge <term>Sey: a fine, durable woolen fabric</term> in shifting colors of green and red, and she had a train. She seemed to play up and down... and seemed to go in and out behind my books, which were lying in heaps. Even as she passed between the largest heaps, the books seemed to make enough room for her, moving apart from one another while she passed between them. And so I considered... the various reports which Edward Kelley made to me of this pretty maiden, and... 

Δ. I said: "Whose girl are you?" 

She: "Whose man are you?" 

Δ. "I am the servant of God, both by my bound duty and also, I hope, by His adoption." 

A voice: "You will be beaten if you tell." 

She: "Am I not a fine maiden? Give me leave to play in your house; my mother told me she would come and dwell here." 

Δ. She went up and down with the very lively gestures of a young girl, playing by herself. Several times, another voice spoke to her from the corner of my study near a large crystal lens <term>Perspective-glass: a mirror or crystal used for scrying (seeing spirits)</term>, but no one was seen besides herself. 

She: "Shall I? I will." (Now she seemed to answer someone in the aforementioned corner of the study.) "I pray you, let me stay a little." <gloss>Speaking to someone in the aforementioned corner</gloss> 

Δ. "Tell me who you are?" 

She: "I pray you, let me play with you a little, and I will tell you who I am." <margin>G4 Jesus</margin> 

Δ. "In the name of Jesus, then, tell me." 

She: "I rejoice in the name of Jesus. I am a poor little maiden, Madini. I am the last but one of my mother’s children. I have little baby-children <note>original: "Proles ipsius Madini," meaning the offspring of Madini herself</note> at home." 

Δ. "Where is your home?" 

Madini: "I dare not tell you where I live; I shall be beaten." 

Δ. "You shall not be beaten for telling the truth to those who love the truth; all creatures must be obedient to the eternal truth." 

Madini: "I guarantee you I will be obedient. My sisters <note>original: "Madini her six Sisters"</note> say they must all come and live with you."
